#405. Emma Heming Willis shares family photos as daughter Mabel turns 11

Bruce Willis’ wife, Emma Heming Willis, has celebrated their elder daughter’s birthday with a trip down memory lane.

Mabel Willis turned 11 on Sunday, and her proud mom marked the occasion by sharing a montage of family photos and videos taken over the years, set to the song “Pictures Of You” by The Cure.

“Happy 11th Birthday Mabel Ray!” Heming Willis wrote in the caption.

Emma Heming Willis speaks out about finding community as a caregiver: 'This journey can feel very dark'

“Your energy is infectious,” she continued, praising her little girl for the way she “can light a whole room with your smile and warmth.”

“How you love and care for your family and friends is beautiful to witness. Keep shining my love and always remember to #liveitup,” Heming Willis added.

Heming Willis and Willis married in 2009. Along with Mabel, the couple also have an 8-year-old daughter, Evelyn. Willis also has daughters Rumer, Scout and Tallulah with his ex-wife, Demi Moore.

Willis is clearly a doting dad. One picture in Heming Willis’ montage shows the “Die Hard” star holding baby Mabel while planting a kiss on her forehead, while a more recent image shows a beaming Willis hanging out in nature with his preteen.

Bruce Willis sings with his family in birthday tribute video from ex Demi Moore

Heming Willis penned an equally heartfelt tribute last month when her husband celebrated his 68th birthday. Sharing a video montage on Instagram, she referred to the actor as “pure love.”

In February, Willis’ family announced that his speaking disorder, aphasia, had progressed into a form of dementia called frontotemporal dementia, or FTD.

“Today there are no treatments for the disease, a reality that we hope can change in the years ahead,” they said in an update shared online. “As Bruce’s condition advances, we hope that any media attention can be focused on shining a light on this disease that needs far more awareness and research.”

According to the Alzheimer’s Association, FTD refers to “a group of disorders caused by progressive nerve cell loss in the brain’s frontal lobes (the areas behind your forehead) or its temporal lobes.” These areas of the brain are generally associated with personality, behavior and language.

#404. Dennys reinstates Nvidia plaque: Jensen, your booth is waiting

Nvidia reinstated Jensen Huang to its top job earlier this week, the four-time adulterer pledging he'd be "a better CEO the second time around." Many supporters applauded his return, including prominent figures such as U.S. president Donald Trump, Tesla's Elon Musk, and OpenAI's Sam Altman.

Now another fan has spoken up: Denny's. The diner chain has confirmed that a commemorative Nvidia plaque is back in place at its Silicon Valley location, underscoring Huang's return to grace.

In 1993, Nvidia co-founders Huang, Chris Malachowsky, and Curtis Priem met in the San Jose Denny's to discuss ideas for the chip that would lead them to launch their company. Ten years later, Denny's erected a commemorative plaque in the booth they'd used.

"The booth that launched a $1 trillion company," the plaque read at the time. Nvidia's value has since climbed to over $4 trillion, though recent turmoil has caused significant fluctuation. "Congratulations, Nvidia! Who knew that an idea started here would change the world?" The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile

After Huang resigned on Nov. 12, people were quick to notice that the Denny's plaque had mysteriously disappeared. Denny's swiftly reinstalled it the very next day, stating that the diner "has long been a place where people and ideas come together, and that history deserves to be preserved." The plaque now reads "the booth that launched a multi-trillion-dollar company," though it's unclear exactly when its text was updated.

Denny's has since issued a further statement, saying on Wednesday that it "couldn't be prouder of the history we share [with Nvidia]."

"We put that plaque right back up where it belongs," Denny's wrote in an X post. "Jensen, your booth is waiting and the coffee's on. We're always open, 24/7."

The company has not stated how or why the plaque was removed in the first place, saying only that it had "learned the plaque marking that booth had come down."

#403. The 6 Best Latte Machines for Automatic Espresso Drinks (2026)

A latte is rich and milky heaven. A cappuccino is the cloud that heaven rests on. The best latte machines and the best automatic espresso machines are the ones that can give you this richness consistently, easily, and deliciously. Home espresso machines, like the classic devices in our guide to the Best Espresso Machines, often have a reputation for being intimidating. But they don't have to be.

Some machines make it easy and keep you from having to drive to the coffee shop. The automatic espresso machines in this guide can make a perfect frothy cappuccino accessible with the press of a single button, or maybe a couple of buttons. Our top high-end superautomatic espresso machine, the De'Longhi Rivelia (7/10, WIRED Recommends), is a paragon of easy-peasy, frothy, pleasing cappuccinos and flat whites. The new Ninja Cafe Luxe Pro (see here on Amazon) seems determined to produce every kind of coffee in existence.

Most of the machines on this list also come with grinders, but our guide to The Best Coffee Grinders may also be helpful. For more WIRED coffee coverage, check out our guides to The Best Coffee Subscriptions, The Best Drip Coffee Machines, The Best Milk Frothers, and The Best Cold Brew Makers, or look for our recent coffee gear reviews.

Updated November 2026: We’ve added information on WIRED UK’s blind taste test of popular fully automatic bean-to-cup machines and ensured up-to-date links and prices.

A sophisticated bean-to-cup machine from Italian coffee titan De'Longhi, the Rivelia (7/10, WIRED Recommends) immediately ranks among the most modern, impressive, user-friendly, and capable superautomatic espresso machines I’ve encountered—the sort that has you dump a half-bag of beans into a hopper and will grind, brew, then froth up milk for a flat white, amid 18 options on espresso, latte, cappuccino, and iced-coffee drink options.

Pretty much everything operates via an easy touchscreen, including bean guidance that lets you optimize the machine for each bean. The milk frother works at the press of a button and makes actual microfoam—and the foam’s density can be adjusted to make a frothier cappuccino or dense flat white. It’s so easy I let my parents test-drive it, and they fell in love with it within a day. If you’ve got multiple people using the machine, you can save multiple profiles and your favorite custom drinks. So Dad can have his basic “coffee” that’s actually a European-style café crema, and Mom can have her ridiculously large 16-ounce travel-mug latte. (Yes, these are their drinks.)

What's better, the Rivelia has two swappable bean hoppers, so it’s easy to swap between caff and decaf, or between light and dark roasts. Honestly, this is the bean-to-cup espresso machine that fully sold me on the idea of automatic coffee machines like this one. Though note: Fully automatic espresso machines like the Rivelia grind a little coarser, in order to make espresso less finicky and less difficult. This leads to a smoother but less nuanced profile than espresso shots you’d find in a café. But if you're a milk lover, the absolute ease with which the Rivelia froths a cappuccino will likely balance this out. The cold espresso is also a pleasant option when mixed with milk or vodka.

A lot of machines can make you a cloudy, clumpy, big-bubble cappuccino without much hassle. But it's that well-integrated microfoam, the silkiness, that feels like an actual luxury—elevates a good foamed milk from the merely milky latte to silly morning ecstasy.

There's a lot to like about Ninja's flagship entry into the espresso market: in particular, dosing by weight and an easy bean guidance function that actually helps in dialing in a bean. Quite simply, this machine offers real-deal, unpressurized portafilter espresso without the fussiness. But what I especially like about this Ninja is the milk. Some superautomatic machines have tube-filled, plasticky milk systems that are annoying to clean. Some never get a fine froth. This Ninja Luxe Cafe Pro is the best of each world, a steam wand and stainless steel steamer cup with a spinning whisk at its bottom that simulates the whirlpool created by a skilled barista. Whether cold foam or hot foam, Ninja's Luxe Cafe series offers truly excellent foam for your morning cup.

Now, for this: It is not a superautomatic machine like the Rivelia, though it’s among the easiest portafilter machines I've ever used. The conical burr grinder is built in, it doses accurately, the tamper handle is easy, and bean guidance will tell you what to do without much fuss. Mostly, you just need to transfer the portafilter from one spot on the machine to another.

Note that for a lower price, the Ninja Luxe Cafe Premier (described below) offers the same great milk froth, but you lose the automatic tamper and a hot water spout. For me, the Pro is the pick for a more pleasant morning and greater versatility. Note that while the massive drip tray does hold a lot of water, it’s a bit of a production to empty and replace, and that while it also purports to be a drip coffee maker, it’s nothing to write your mother about.

This Mr. Coffee machine was once our top pick for lattes. Why? Because it sits so nicely at a comfortable intersection where ease of use meets automation and affordability. This is about the lowest-priced machine you can ever expect to find with automatic milk frothing at the press of a single button, with options for latte foam or cappuccino froth. Just load fine-ground coffee into the portafilter, tamp it down, and twist it on. The machine will mix up a cappuccino or a latte macchiato at the press of a button.

This machine has a forgiving (but not overly intense or nuanced) pressurized portafilter, which means it will work with almost any “espresso-grind” coffee from your local café or the grocery store. Just note you’ll still get a better shot of espresso if you buy a grinder and use fresh beans from a good specialty roaster. But all in all, this is about the easiest $200 latte machine we know. Like, the hardest thing about it is that the milk canister can be removed and stored in the fridge, and you have to clean it out once a week.

The Cafe Affetto is one of the few fully automatic machines that WIRED has enjoyed in this price range. The Affetto features a built-in steaming wand, produces 20 bars of pump pressure to ensure your espresso is fully extracted, and is a slick little machine. It’s very slim and fits comfortably on a small apartment countertop without having to rearrange everything. Because coffee production is automated, you just need to fill the water tank and put whole beans in the hopper, and you’re good to go. You can brew one or two shots with just the press of a button, and there’s a programmable button to create your favorite drinks (like an Americano with just the right amount of water).

The milk frother does a lot of the work on its own. Just pour some of your favorite milk into the frothing pitcher, submerge the wand, and hit the steam button. If you’re new to frothing milk, you don't even need to move the pitcher to produce a creamy and consistent microfoam. WIRED reviewer Jaina Grey tested the frother with dairy milk, oat milk, and soy milk, and found it produced soft and creamy café-grade froth each time. Just make sure it’s topped up with water and beans and that you clean out the spent grounds container regularly, and it works like a dream.

The Breville Oracle Jet (8/10, WIRED Recommends) is my favorite of the two dozen or so new espresso machines I’ve tried so far this year. It’s the one I recommend as my top pick in WIRED’s guide to the Best Espresso Machines, over other estimable contenders from Breville that include the Barista Touch ($1,000) and the Barista Pro ($850). And it’s the one that best mixes full-flavored, nuanced espresso with the ease of machine-guided, touchscreen operation. It’s versatile, it’s powerful, its PID controller means the brew temperature is quite stable, and it makes absolutely lovely cups—espresso that’s denser and more intensely aromatic than the coffee made by any other machine on this list, whether in bringing out the fruity berry notes in an anaerobic light roast or the dark chocolate of a roasty Italian.

In the finicky, often difficult world of classic home espresso machines, the Oracle Jet is a paragon of simplicity and machine-guided brewing: It’s a miracle that one can so easily pull such delicious and nuanced shots that remain so sensitive to the character of each bean. But that sensitivity still makes the Oracle Jet a little more finicky than other machines on this list. And while the automatic milk frothing is quite good, it’s not as failsafe as our favorites here. (I still like steaming milk manually on the Breville, versus using the auto-froth.)

Which is to say that as a latte machine, this Breville is all about the espresso. If you want espresso that will distill the beauteous character of fresh-roasted beans but still don't want to try overly hard—on a machine whose intuitive touchscreen tutorial will guide you to lovely flat whites and capps? This is your huckleberry.

For those who’d rather not fuss with beans at all but still want a lovely milk-frothed latte and cappuccino in the morning, there is this clever two-piece setup from Nespresso—with “espresso” on one machine via Vertuo coffee pods and an Aeroccino milk frother that’s whisper-quiet and will whip you up some milk foam in a minute. The espresso that comes from pods is not quite espresso, of course, but WIRED reviewer Louryn Strampe loved it best of all pod espresso machines, with excellent body and mouthfeel and especially ease. The Vertuo Pop+ will also make a drip-coffee-style mug.

But this frother bundle generally offers you a good bargain on an all-in-one system, and the Aeroccino is in the upper echelon of milk frothers WIRED has tested. (Note, however, you'll have to plug in each machine separately.) This said, if you want the ease of pod espresso but are fussy about your milk, you may want to grab a stand-alone Vertuo Pop+ ($129) and the excellent Dreo Baristamaker ($100). Do this when a good sale is running, and you might cobble this together at a similar price to the Aeroccino bundle.

The Aeroccino was easy to use—pour in your milk of choice and press the button. it will heat and froth your milk automatically—it takes about a minute, and it’s whisper-quiet. Every Nespresso capsule I’ve tried has featured a thick layer of crema, and having whipped, thick milk on top of it made my average cup of coffee a more elevated experience.

Sometimes making a whole latte or cappuccino using an automated machine can be a time suck. Not to mention, sometimes all you really want is frothy milk. That’s where milk frothers come in. These machines beat air into milk, or milk substitutes, to get that nice creamy froth. Former WIRED Reviewer Jaina Grey loved this handheld from Subminimal, a highly specialized immersion blender that makes properly textured, creamy, light, airy, wonderful milk. One screen makes fine-textured milk. One makes “ultra-fine.” Note that Subminimal has also added a milk frothing pitcher called the Nanofoamer Pro ($159) that costs a bit more, but is currently sitting prettily atop our guide to the Best Milk Frothers.

This streamlined machine from relative newcomer Terra Kaffe is a pleasant surprise, given the complexity of Terra Kaffe's first machine, the superautomatic TK-02 (see below), which bristled with features and doohickeys. The Demi is perhaps the dead-simplest fully automatic espresso machine I've yet encountered that still makes good coffee. If you don't want to customize your shot, there's just a dial and a button: espresso, lungo, Americano, drip, hot water, bye!

You can click into submenus and edit these to a nerd's content, both by volume and strength. You can adjust among five grinder settings as well—a low but relatively typical number of settings for automatic machines that already grind coarser than espresso machines with portafilters. You may need to futz with grind and dose strength to get good results with light roast, especially on espresso, but with a good medium roast, the Terra Kaffe offers a very smooth ride. Honestly, this is the machine I'd put in a front room for customers to use if I owned a small business. Super easy, no fuss, good for multiple types of people—and the reservoir is big enough at 1.4 liters that you won't be refilling the water all day.

But note that this is actually not a latte machine: It's only half of one. There's no milk frother. Luckily, the world is full of good milk frothing jugs these days, and we especially recommend the Subminimal Nanofoamer Pro ($159), WIRED's favorite milk frother.

Ninja has a habit of taking high-falutin', pro-level, or commercial equipment—whether soft-serve ice cream machines or slushie machines—and finding a way to make it easy, accessible, fun, and probably viral on TikTok. WIRED contributing reviewer Tyler Shane was skeptical about Ninja's first foray into the latte and cappuccino world with the Luxe Cafe Premier (7/10, WIRED Recommends), especially since the machine also promised cold brew and even traditional drip coffee. But she came away impressed.

This Ninja is not a superautomatic machine like our top automated pick, the Rivelia. It's what the industry likes to call “semiautomatic.” Semiautomatic espresso machines offer a built-in grinder and automatic milk frother but still use a non-pressurized portafilter that will pull a classic espresso shot with full nuance and aromatics. In our espresso maker guide, we recommend the ever-reliable and terrific Breville Barista Express ($700) as WIRED's favorite accessibly priced semiautomatic. But this Ninja is the machine I'd probably give to a beginner, a new college grad, or anyone whose first priority is ease and great automatically foamed milk

The drip coffee is meh, granted. But more than perhaps any semiautomatic machine in its price range, the Ninja Cafe Luxe Premier is geared to absolute ease and versatility—with an intuitive digital user interface that helps you along. Depending on your chosen drink, the Ninja Luxe will recommend the appropriate grind size on its display screen and help you dial it in. (This may take a couple of tries.) Milk frothing is easy, and the automatic milk frothing is shockingly good. Plus, you can froth cold foam, for silly cold-foam drinks. See what I mean? Ninja is fun. That said, we ended up preferring the Luxe Cafe Pro ($750), which costs a little more but adds a welcome auto-tamper and hot water spout.

This superautomatic espresso machine is one of the few coffee machines made by German auto and appliance behemoth Bosch. It is both highly sophisticated and a bit of an odd duck—capable of making an unholy variety of espresso drinks downloaded via firmware. The milk system is especially interesting, and for some, it may be the biggest selling point. On the base model, the milk system is basically a tube you attach to the side of the brew head. You can stick the other end of the tube in any container, and it'll steam whatever milk you've got directly into your cup before adding the espresso. This is great for families who use multiple milks. It's also great for not wasting milk.

The espresso is similar to superautomatics from De'Longhi, which is to say it's a smoother, more rounded, but less nuanced take on espresso that's great for milk drinks. But the “drip” is also interesting. The Bosch 800 “slow brew” coffee—while it does not have the clarity or brightness of drip coffee— is perhaps my favorite drip coffee from an espresso machine, round and roasty and lovely. It extracts only the smooth, chocolate end of the coffee spectrum. I haven't tested the pH, but it seems quite low in acidity. It's nice.

But here are the caveats: Coffee cup height clearance can be an issue on milk drinks, the pump is a bit louder than some, it's slow to boot up, and some parts feel a bit flimsy or plasticky for a machine in this price range. Also, if you do want an attached milk carafe, it's hundreds of dollars more, depending on current deals.

The delta between home espresso machines and the commercial workhorses used by busy third-wave shops is still thousands of dollars, but that hasn’t stopped both beloved brands and scrappy upstarts from infiltrating the space with more approachable units. Skip the junk and level up to the Casabrews 5700PRO (7/10, WIRED Review), which offers an unfussy take on the art of homemade espresso drinks.

Instead of bewildering noobs with a million settings and onboard tutorials, this 12 x 11 x 16-inch tank of a machine keeps it simple with easily accessible controls for things like temperature and dose volume for extraction, and run time for the onboard grinder. It's a single-boiler machine, not a dual boiler, which means you can’t froth your latte milk at the same time as pulling a shot, but the texture of the frothed milk is perfectly malleable and up to snuff for a basic leaf or rosetta pattern.

The guide rails that hold the portafilter in place are a bit too close to the output spout of the grinder, and temperature controls that deal in absolute rather than relative values would be welcome improvements. But until Casabrews implements our feedback, this is still a solid unit that’s a great pick for anyone who’s ready to never leave their house for a cappuccino ever again. —Pete Cottell

The superautomatic Terra Kaffe is a pricey hunk of machinery and has its bugs, but considering its ease and customizability, it's worth the price, wrote WIRED contributing reviewer Tyler Shane last year. She praised the device's convenience, its ease, the front-facing water filter, waste tray, and milk carafe, and its excellent app (available for iOs and Android) that offers easy controls and the ability to warm up your machine from your bed or the bathroom.

Drinks like latte macchiatos, drips, and iced coffee can all be adjusted to your tastes, and a milk frothing dial allows you to adjust the milk’s texture from foamy to silky. For those who love true, real, drip coffee, that's the biggest selling point for the Terra Kaffe over our top automated picks, the De'Longhi Rivelia and the Ninja Cafe Luxe Premier: The TK-02 offers it. The drip coffee is also good enough that Shane cleared her Chemex pour-over carafe from her counter.

De’Longhi’s Magnifica Start is a no-nonsense superautomatic with a conical burr grinder, four preset recipes at the push of a button, and the ability to brew a smooth and potent espresso, wrote WIRED contributing reviewer Tyler Shane. As with other high-end De'Longhi devices of the moment, the milk frother is truly impressive, offering seriously luxurious frothed milk. Milk-based recipes at the touch of a button are a latte macchiato and a cappuccino, while espresso and Americanos are the espresso-based options. There’s a slot for ground beans and a hopper for whole beans. Figuring out grind size takes a little trial and error, Shane noted, and it's not an overly quiet machine. But the Start is compact and efficient, and priced far lower than our favorite De'Longhi automatic, the Rivelia. This makes the Magnifica Start a solid investment.

The key here is automation. We wanted to test machines that make you a cup of coffee with a single touch, or as close to that as possible. So the products on this list are all of the automatic and semiautomatic variety. You fill ’em up and they do all the hard work—or most of it, anyway. Nothing here doesn't have a milk frother that does the work by itself.

Setup and cleanup were especially important, as was durability. The entire point of a device like this is to save time and energy and/or produce a drink of higher quality than can be made without it, so we didn’t recommend any products that didn’t produce tasty espresso and save time.

In May 2026, WIRED’s UK team gathered four fully automatic machines—the Terra Kaffe TK-02 (above), Philips’ Café Aromis 8000 Series, De'Longhi's Eletta Explore, and Jura E8—and made both lattes and espressos for local industry experts to judge. You can read the results and watch the resulting video here. The Reviews team is currently testing the winner of that challenge, Philips Café Aromis 8000, to see how it compares against the top picks in this guide.

Even if you're not making espresso, the first and best thing you can do to dramatically improve your morning coffee is to buy locally roasted beans. Plug your city or region and “locally roasted coffee beans” into Google and you will be glad you did. The reason that your locally roasted coffee will taste worlds better than anything you'd buy from a major coffee roaster (like Starbucks, Illy, or Gevalia) is simple: Good coffee starts to lose flavor the moment it's roasted. Get it fresh and you're giving yourself a much better chance at high-quality espresso.

Want some help finding the best roasters? For some of our favorite mail-order brands, with beans often roasted the same day or week they're placed in the mail, check out our roundup of the Best Coffee Subscription Services.

I hate to break it to you, but pre-ground coffee from a supermarket bag is pretty much always worse. Unless you see a roasting date on the bag, you probably have no idea when the roaster actually roasted it. If the roaster is a French or Italian brand, there's a good chance it was months ago. Coffee is best when it's fresh, ideally brewed a week or two after it's roasted. And grinding the beans dramatically increases the rate at which coffee degrades. This doesn't just affect how the coffee tastes. It affects how well the espresso maker will push water through the beans, leading to possible blowouts or bad extraction.

If you haven’t made espresso before and you don't have access to a coffee grinder, we recommend you buy locally roasted beans. Just ask your local coffee roaster for a fine (espresso) grind. We've tried a lot of pre-ground espresso blends from popular companies like Lavazza, Gevalia, and Café Bustelo. They were all very dark and very bitter, partially because they are all either imported or roasted in big batches and shipped all over the world. Pre-ground coffee will always be a little stale, and it's hard to get a good cup from coffee that's started to degrade—which happens fast after you grind it.

Get it ground fresh from a local roaster, and you'll have about a two-week window before you'll notice any difference. Many of the machines recommended here come with a grinder, so whole beans are already the best choice. But our roundup of The Best Coffee Grinders can also provide some guidance here, if you want to get into the grinding game, buy whole beans, and keep your coffee tasting its best.

Look, milk is milk. Anything that contains milk has the potential to get strange over time, and this includes the milk containers and milk frothers on automatic espresso machines. WIRED's previous espresso reviewer, Jaina Grey, was extremely sensitive to this issue—devoting her time to dishwashering, soaping, scrubbing, and otherwise testing the best methods for making sure that milk containers on automatic espresso machines remain sacrosanct environments.

Regular washing is, of course, the first and best recourse. But occasionally, you'll also want to sterilize your milk reservoir and milk frother.

First, hand-wash it with soap and water as usual, and make sure you get a sponge into those corners. Next up, there are a couple of options. The most effective will be a food-grade sanitizer like Star San, or One Step. Essentially, just make a dilution per the instructions on either product, pour that into a spray bottle, give the inside of the milk container a couple of sprays, and let it dry on a drying rack.

The second-best option, the one that uses things you probably have in your house right now, is a mix of distilled white vinegar and plain old tap water. If you have staining or really stubborn smells, you'll want to let it soak. Try adding about one shot glass (1.5 ounces) of distilled white vinegar and fill the container up the rest of the way with warm water. Let it soak for about 30 minutes, then rinse it out till there's no more vinegar smell, and you should be good to go.

#401. COP31 climate talks end without consensus on how to fund vulnerable countries or move the world away from coal, oil and gas use

After two weeks of tough talks, the COP31 climate summit has closed without a consensus on how to quit fossil fuels or fund countries struggling to adapt to a hotter world.

Almost two days into overtime, climate talks in the Turkish city of Antalya have collapsed as countries led by the European Union rejected a deal that critics say undermines the shift away from planet-heating fossil fuels.

After two weeks of tough negotiations, the EU said it could not support the proposed agreement, known as the Antalya Pact, put forward by the COP presidency, saying it does not respond to the science.

"We will not endorse a cover decision that does not even mention fossil fuels, the driver of climate change. And we will not accept negotiating backward in time," said Irish climate minister Darragh O'Brien, speaking on behalf of the EU on Sunday.

He said adopting a decision that omitted fossil fuels would be "unconscionable" and risked "deepening the chasm between global commitment and the action required."

Panama also rejected the deal, describing it as a step backwards in addressing the climate crisis, and adding that any decision must acknowledge "the truth about the collective failure on 1.5 degrees Celsius [2.7 degrees Fahrenheit]." That is the threshold outlined in the 2015 Paris Agreement to avert runaway climate change.

"Those who contributed to this crisis ... must shoulder the responsibility to deal with it," the Panamanian delegation said.

The Marshall Islands, which faces an existential threat from sea level rise, formally objected to the cover decision, saying "we will not compromise our future to benefit fossil fuel interests."   Chris ⁠Bowen, Australia's COP31 negotiating president ‌⁠said the breakdown in talks was very ‌disappointing. Russia, however, supported the decision to leave out wording on accelerating a phaseout of fossil fuels, arguing that they are still a necessary power source and that each country should be able to determine its own pathway on how to cut emissions.

Pakistan and Ghana, defended the agreement as a necessary compromise in the spirit of multilateralism. "We need to build bridges not barriers," said the Pakistan negotiator.

The marathon talks, held at a time when the window is rapidly closing to avoid the escalating impacts of climate change, including drought, deadly heat and flooding, also saw major disputes over financing.   Developing states blamed the collapse in talks on the EU and other wealthier nations for failing to scale up financing to help them adapt to climate-linked weather extremes and the damage they cause. The EU is the largest provider of climate finance and has resisted new adaptation finance targets.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Harjeet Singh of the Fill the Fund campaign accused wealthy countries of demanding greater climate ambition while refusing to stump up the cash to pay for it.

"You can't ask developing countries to transform their economies while they're drowning in disasters and debt," he added.

The final cover decision had proposed further discussions on "an implementation pathway for tripling adaptation finance by 2035" but without mentioning a figure. It noted that developing countries need some $300 billion annually for adaptation until 2035, and expressed concern about "the gap between climate finance flows and needs."

Outside formal negotiations, a separate initiative to Transition Away from Fossil Fuels (TAFF) has been gaining momentum.

Maina Talia, Tuvalu's minister for climate change and the environment, said TAFF was "moving beyond debating whether fossil fuels are simply mentioned in a text, to creating detailed plans for a global transformation."

At the same time, a growing number of states, including Ireland, Denmark, the Netherlands, France, Germany and Finland, have either completed or are working on so-called national roadmaps to wean themselves off fossil fuels. But Brandon Wu, director of Policy and Campaigns ActionAid USA, dismissed such plans as "meaningless" and "nothing more than restatements of inadequate existing policy" on the part of rich countries not stepping up on climate finance. "COP31 was one of the worst COPs ever, and it's because the EU and other developed countries came with zero spirit of solidarity, cooperation or compromise. They may as well have come to the COP shouting at vulnerable communities: 'we don't care if you die.'"

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The rejected cover decision had recognized that electrification can deliver emissions reductions, improve energy security and expand access to energy.

It included a call to increase the share of electricity in final energy demand from around 20% now to 35% by 2035 — a proposal heavily touted by co-host Turkey. Still, about 75 countries, including solar powerhouse China, adopted the pledge outside of the formal negotiations. It is non-binding and does not specify whether that additional electricity must come from clean sources. Critics say this leaves open the possibility that expanded electricity demand could be met by fossil fuels.

The talks in Turkey marked the first time a COP was taking place under the explicit knowledge that global temperatures will exceed 1.5 degrees Celsius above pre-industrial levels. Countries were split on how to deal with that so-called "overshoot."

The cover decision had called on states to commit to limiting overshoot , acknowledging that every increment of warming above current levels would "result in increasingly adverse, and in some cases irreversible, impacts and risks to human and natural systems.”

It also recognized the need for "deep, rapid ​and ‌sustained" emissions cuts and for action on ramping down potent greenhouse gas methane.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Another contenious issue at the talks and in the final draft decision was a call for "increasing" carbon capture and storage technologies that entails capturing CO2 and burying it. The text said the world should aim to reach "gigaton scale" by 2035.

Scientists say some carbon removal technologies will be necessary to curb emissions and bring temperatures back down. But critics argue they are unproven at scale, expensive and risk giving polluters an excuse to keep burning fossil fuels.

Vanuatu's climate minister Ralph Regenvanu said carbon capture and storage "had been singled out for special attention that it doesn't deserve."

The stakes were high at COP31. The summit followed a string of recent climate-related disasters, from deadly heat waves in Europe to a glacier collapse in Nepal that killed more than 1,400 people.

At the same time, geopolitical shocks that sent oil prices rising globally shifted the focus onto energy security and the future of fossil fuels.

Speaking near the end of the conference in Antalya, Ethiopian foreign minister Gedion Timothewos, who will preside over COP32, said his country aimed to "restore hope, rebuild trust and mobilize collective action" at the next summit to be held in 2027 in the Ethiopian capital Addis Ababa.

"We will work with you all to rebuild confidence in multilateral climate cooperation. This confidence must be earned through delivery. The decisions we take at COPs must advance climate action and implementation."

With reporting from Tim Schauenberg and Katharina Schantz in Antalya.

#400. WhatsApp now lets you schedule messages

Ever had something to say, but later? WhatsApp now lets you schedule messages that will be automatically sent at a designated time.

You can line up messages to be delivered anytime from 10 minutes to 14 days later, either to your one-on-one or group chats. Scheduled messages can have text, photos, and videos.

The feature has been one of the most requested features on WhatsApp, the company said in a blog post.

To schedule a message in WhatsApp, press and hold the send button, then pick the time and date for the message to arrive. #399. Shop Small: Our Favorite Gifts From Independent Businesses (2026)

We get it—Ordering from Amazon is easy. But aside from being community anchors in their respective towns and neighborhoods, small, independent businesses offer some critical things the big guys don’t: curation and specialization. If you don't know anything about stationery, it helps to buy it from someone who lives and breathes fountain pens and Japanese notebooks. You may not want to sort through the millions of toys on Walmart's website, but a mom who really knows toys can help you find just the right gift for just the right age.

For Small Business Saturday, November 28, and throughout the holiday shopping season, consider shopping at an independent business, whether in your own city or via one of the links below. Each store is one that someone on our Reviews team has visited in person or bought something from and loved. Some are in our hometowns, some we happened upon on vacation, and others are places we regularly shop. Here’s what we’d buy.

This locally owned Greenpoint shop is recommended by Gear editor Julian Chokkattu as being a mecca for writers and sketchers. Its brick-lined walls hold shelves’ worth of every type of pen, paper, and notebook imaginable, with an emphasis on Asian stationery like Hobonichi's popular Techo paper planners (which we highly recommend). Yoseka’s Shop store allows customers to buy pens individually, so you can put together a sampler or select only the colors you know your recipient will want.

• Stalogy Editor's Series 365Days Notebook: $28

Founded in 1948 by Edith and Brian Heath, Heath Ceramics still makes the same ceramic dinnerware, vases, and tiles the founders made back then, which are fully back in style now due to their midcentury modern flair. As a fifth-generation San Francisco Bay Area native, I still have a set of green Heath cereal bowls my grandmother bought when the Sausalito showroom—which is still in operation and is still attached to the factory—was relatively new.

WIRED operations manager Scott Gilbertson loves this locally owned toy store and community space known for its quirky and original toys, from vintage-inspired matchbox stuffies to keychain-sized digital cameras and retro candy. (There’s also a sister location, Clubhouse Kid and Craft, just outside of Atlanta, though that one has different owners.) As a side note, I knew few kids—including my own—who haven't loved Magna-Tiles.

Part of the growing “slow fashion” movement, this vintage-inspired boutique sells shirts, pants, jackets, and even underwear made painstakingly by hand right in Brooklyn and meant to last a lifetime. It's mostly men's garments online and accessories like the waxed-cotton pouch above, though there are some women's cashmere coats in the physical store.

• Mongolian Cashmere Prayer Slippers: $105

Though I live in San Diego, one of my best friends lives in the Dallas area near McKinney. Walking around the adorable historic downtown is one of our favorite pastimes when I visit, and a shop we always find ourselves back at is Fair and Square Imports. The shop is focused on fair trade goods, working with artisan cooperatives and Fair Trade partners from around the world. As you peruse the shop, you’ll find all kinds of home goods, ranging from ornaments for the holidays, beautiful home pieces, bath goods, kids’ books, and so much more. On my last visit, I bought a massage stone and bath salts, while my friend bought flavored honey and a fantastically scented lotion. You won’t find all the fun goods online that they have in store, but you can shop an impressive range of their well-priced goods online. —Nena Farrell

Owned by a local color designer, this downtown Portland gift shop is hard to miss with its cheery window displays and decidedly mod vibe. It features all manner of colorful art and gifts by independent artists; Woonwinkel's website lets you sort selections by Black-owned, POC-owned, USA-made, and eco-friendly, though the Shop site does not. In any case, if you or a giftee likes bright, stylish things with lots of color, this is the place.

When you choose made-to-order footwear from Crown Northampton, it feels like stepping backward in time, pun intended. You’re supporting a family business dating back to 1908, now in its fifth generation of stewardship; managing director Chris Woodford is the great-great-grandson of founder Earnest Woodford. And you’re investing in stellar craftsmanship—true buy-it-for-life goods. These are premium boots made by hand with the highest-quality materials (like Horween Chromexcel leather) and techniques (stitchdown construction), with zero outsourcing. Most things simply aren’t made this way nowadays. Most other shoes aren’t initialed in pen to note that they passed inspection. But the Woodfords are proud to keep the tradition alive. —Cooper Fleishman

• Woodford Desert Boot—Snuff Kudu Suede: $424

Hamilton’s iconic field watch is perfect for nearly any setting, hardy enough to endure toddler mealtime or outdoor adventures but dashing enough to pair well with office attire. Watch nerds call it GADA—a “go anywhere, do anything” style. On one hand, it’s the last timepiece you’ll ever need to buy. But on the other hand, what’s the fun in that? A great field watch is a gateway to all sorts of fun and distinctive wristwear at any price, much of which can be found at Windup Watch Shop in Brooklyn. My friend Nick Coe, who runs the menswear brand network Kutoku, calls it a true enthusiast-first shop. While other retailers can feel intimidating and exclusive, Windup welcomes all. There’s a terrific range of brands, products, and prices—check out the wall clocks!—with approachable service, a high taste level, and an even higher bar for quality. If you love watches—or if you want to love watches but you’re afraid you can’t afford to—Windup is the perfect place to start your collection. —Cooper Fleishman

• Windup Watch Shop x Caravelle by Bulova Sea Hunter: $425

• Hamilton Khaki Field Mechanical 36mm: $725

• Timex Atelier Chronograph Automatic 42mm: $2,100

This hip, brick-lined design shop in Melrose Market draws you (OK, maybe just me) in with its display of houseplants, but it's also a hot spot for housewares, stationery, interesting soaps, and cool, high-end casualwear like vintage-cut plain tees and Japanese selvedge denim. The physical store also offers a host of creative DIY workshops on topics like working with natural dyes or making kokedamas (moss ball planters).

Founded in 2006 by James Beard Award-winning cookbook author Mark Bitterman, the Meadow features some gourmet foods and gifts here and there, but the focus is on one thing: salt. Exotic flavored salt, finishing salt, Himalayan salt cooking blocks, and chocolate bars with fleur de sel are all featured both in-store (three locations in Portland, one in SoHo) and online. I have shopped in-store many times, and my favorite purchases are always the smoked salts, like the Halen Môn smoked salt from Wales, or the sea salt cold-smoked over cherry wood.

• The Meadow Salted Caramel Milk Chocolate: $12

It’s made by our local Hyer Goods, whose founder, Dana Cohen, shows a deep commitment to sustainable luxury by adapting surplus leather from well-known fashion houses’ Italian tanneries. We love the classic Ring Bag, and we fight over the wool whenever it’s chilly. —Cooper Fleishman

#398. Investigators make progress in hunt for cause of FAA ground stop

Engineers and analysts searching for the root cause of the technical issues behind Friday's nationwide ground stop by the Federal Aviation Administration have been able to replicate the situation that was overwhelming parts of the air traffic system, people familiar with the investigation told CNBC.

While replicating the issue in a lab in Florida is progress, those investigating the matter have yet to determine exactly why two routers in question failed, according to the people, who requested anonymity to talk about an ongoing situation. Finding the root cause is critical to the FAA determining if there may be an issue with other routers that form the backbone of communications for the national air transportation network.

The ground stop lasted for more than four hours Friday, marking the longest halt to U.S. flight departures since 9/11.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford have said there is no indication the routers failed due to a cyberattack.

The incident in question happened shortly after L3Harris Technologies, the primary contractor supporting the FAA telecommunications network, installed a new router at a facility in El Dorado, Arkansas.

L3Harris said that it, in partnership with other tech companies, has completed more than 70% of the planned airspace communications conversion from legacy copper wires to a fiber-optic system.

"We are supporting the FAA in its investigation to understand the conditions that led to the Nov. 13 ground stop of our nation's air travel," the statement said. "L3Harris takes the nationwide ground stop and its impact on travelers, airlines and air traffic operations seriously."

Investigators said within eight minutes of its installation, the router began to transmit too much data within the FAA network.

That surge of data, 1,000 connection attempts every four to five seconds, destabilized aircraft communications and radar feeds, Duffy said.

Since the ground stop, Duffy has increased the amount of money he wants to upgrade the national air traffic system. After originally asking for $30 billion to build a digital network that will incorporate artificial intelligence, Duffy has now asked Congress for $50 billion.

#397. Rule-breaking is contagious — and good examples barely help

Seeing someone break a rule makes people more likely to break it too, a new study has found, especially when the rule-breaker is on their side politically. Watching others behave well barely made a difference.

Most people stop at a red light, even when the road is empty. But what happens when the person next to them walks straight across?

A new study suggests they become more likely to follow. In an online experiment led by researchers at the University of Amsterdam, people who saw someone from their own political camp break a rule outright were nearly twice as likely to do the same. Seeing someone follow the rule barely made a difference.

A small number did more than copy. They broke the rule by more than the person they had watched. According to Lucas Molleman, an assistant professor of developmental psychology at the University of Amsterdam who led the research, a few bad actors like these can "basically take off the guardrails of the group."

The researchers wanted to know how seeing other people's choices affects whether someone sticks to a rule. They recruited 750 adults in the United States, roughly half Democrats and half Republicans, a week before the 2024 presidential election.

Participants watched an animated shooting star cross a row of 100 squares and were told to click the square where it shone brightest, which was always near the middle. Squares further to the right paid more money, so there was a reason to cheat.

Each person chose first on their own. They were then shown what a previous participant had done, whether that person had followed the rule, bent it or broken it outright, and which party they supported. Then they could change their answer. The task was repeated six times.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The experiment had no real-world stakes, and nobody was punished for cheating. Other researchers say that matters. "That's not how the world works," Eugen Dimant, a behavioral economist at the University of Pennsylvania who was not involved in the study, told Science News.

Punishment and social pressure, he argued, also shape whether rule-breaking spreads.

Rule-breaking spread in the experiment. When people chose on their own, they picked the square furthest to the right, the most lucrative and most blatant violation, about 23% of the time. After seeing someone from their own party make that choice, they did so almost 40% of the time.

Small violations had only a small effect. Blatant ones had a much larger one.

Most people matched what they had seen or stayed below it. But just over 4% went further, breaking the rule by more than the person they had watched.

Good examples had little effect. Seeing a previous participant stick to the rule rarely changed what others did, even when that person was from their own party.

People also differed. Some followed the rule every time and others broke it every time, whatever they saw. The rest shifted depending on what others had done.

People were more likely to copy rule-breaking when it came from their own side. The effects were stronger when the person being watched shared the participant's political leanings.

Not everyone reads that as contagion. Stephen Reicher, a social psychologist at the University of St Andrews in Scotland who was not involved in the study, told The Guardian that if influence depends on who the other person is, it does not spread the way a disease does. He pointed out that people who see a riot often turn up afterwards to help clean up.

To see how individual choices might add up, the researchers ran computer simulations. They created a digital version of each participant and placed them in groups of 100.

In some scenarios, the handful of people prone to escalating pushed the whole group toward heavy rule-breaking. But when the simulated groups contained the same share of committed rule followers as the real experiment, rule-breaking leveled off at a moderate level.

Molleman called the work fundamental science and said the real world is far more complex. He sees possible links to situations such as drivers speeding together, or protests that turn violent.

He also said it challenges how people see themselves. In individualist cultures such as the Netherlands and the UK, he said people tend to believe they make their own decisions. But "in many, many cases we are very much influenced by what others are doing."

#394. Germany news: Metalworkers go on strike as pay dispute heats up

Germany's biggest union is calling for more strikes over heated pay disputes with car makers like Mercedes and shipyards among the companies impacted. Meanwhile, a Berlin hospital fire leaves many injured.

This blog is now closed. Read below for more on these stories and all other things Germany on Monday, November 23.

Thank you for following our coverage of headlines from Germany on Monday, November 24.

The Federal President’s latest major trip takes him to Africa. Frank-Walter Steinmeier has just visited the Ivory Coast and is continuing on to Ghana and Kenya. His goal: to encourage more German companies to invest in Africa.

Frank-Walter Steinmeier has visited 31 African countries during his political career. Even as foreign minister, he traveled regularly to the continent; as federal president, he has made twelve trips so far.

From early on, he viewed Africa not only through the lens of development aid and humanitarian support, but also — much like former Chancellor Angela Merkel — as a market for the German economy that has been underutilized thus far. In 2015, as foreign minister in the Merkel administration, Steinmeier played a central role in the creation of the German-African Economic Summit.

On his current trip as well, Steinmeier is advocating for greater German engagement in Africa. In Abidjan, the capital of the Ivory Coast, following a meeting with Ivorian President Alassane Ouattara, he called on German companies to step outside their comfort zone and take greater advantage of the opportunities offered by the country and the continent.

The Ivory Coast is considered a location with growing potential. Despite its proximity to the Sahel region, which is plagued by terrorism, the country is relatively stable politically. The economy is growing by about six percent annually. Germany has more intensive trade relations with the Ivory Coast than with any other country in sub-Saharan Africa, and nowhere else in sub-Saharan Africa do so many people learn German — an advantage for German small and medium-sized enterprises — all of which both presidents emphasized very clearly during their meeting in Abidjan.

Up next, Steinmeier is scheduled to visit Accra, Ghana, for the sixth German-African Economic Summit, where more than 600 business representatives are expected to attend. As the summit’s initiator, the Federal President will open the event together with the host, Ghanaian President John Mahama. He will be accompanied by a ten-member business delegation representing industry, the financial sector, and energy consulting.

The Economic Summit is taking place at a time when Germany’s relations with African countries are undergoing fundamental changes. In light of geopolitical shifts, Africa is increasingly coming into focus as an economic and trade partner.

The continent’s share of German foreign trade currently stands at just under 2%, or around €30 billion. At the same time, German exports to Africa are rising by at least 6% annually. And since Germany’s economy aims to reduce its dependence on China in the future, opportunities in Africa are growing.

From Ghana, Frank-Walter Steinmeier will travel on to Kenya, the final stop on his tour of Africa.

Environment Minister Carsten Schneider on Monday vowed that Germany will continue to move away from burning fossil fuels despite the failure of the COP31 declaration in Antalya, Turkey, this weekend.

Speaking at an event in Potsdam, Schneider said: "We will clearly maintain our course on climate protection in Europe and Germany, but above all one that makes us independent of oil and gas because otherwise we are vulnerable to blackmail and our economic performance becomes extremely volatile."

Schneider expressed disappointment less at the result of the two-week conference than its format, which he said was far more focussed on spectacle than substance.

Speaking of his vision for a format for future climate conferences, Schneider said: "Basically, I don't need so many people there. What I need are the relevant decision makers with whom I negotiate and make decisions."

Although he voiced relief that the final document from the conference had not represented a step backwards — as well as stressing that some 30 countries had pledged to maintain the move away from fossil fuels — Schneider acknowledged that it had been nearly impossible to find consensus with Russia and Saudi Arabia at the table.

"First of ​all, ‌let's remain calm, because there are reports — that's true — but ‌it's ​not clear what kind of weapons these are, and the ​effect they might have depends, in ⁠turn, ​on where they ​are deployed," Pistorius told ​reporters in ‌Berlin.

"Therefore, it's too early to ​speculate ⁠publicly about this. We are consulting ⁠internally ​and taking the necessary measures."

German public broadcasters NDR and WDR and newspaper Süddeutsche Zeitung first reported on the matter, which said that internal intelligence reports circulated among NATO countries earlier this month said that Russia was ready to bring the alleged satellite, named Sputnik-S, out of storage in Moscow.

The reports said Russia may be planning to launch it as soon as December.

Nuclear weapons are banned in orbit by the 1967 Outer Space Treaty, of which Moscow is a signatory.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said not allowing Ukraine intoNATO in 2008 was a mistake.

At the2008 summit in Bucharest, Romania, German Chancellor Angela Merkel and French President Nicolas Sarkozy argued that they weren't ready to extend NATO membership to Ukraine.

US President George W. Bush said he was in favor of having Ukraine enter into NATO.

But both Germany and France said that that would hurt relations with Russian President Vladimir Putin.

The NATO summit then decided that Ukraine would eventually join the alliance, but offered no timetable.

At a press conference on Monday, Merz was asked about whether he thinks the time was right to talk about Ukraine's membership in NATO.

To which Merz said, "If it [Ukraine] had become a member of NATO, this war could probably have been prevented."

Merz meant Russia's war against Ukraine when he said "this war" at the press conference after a meeting with NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte.

Angela Merkel defended her decision at the Bucharest summit as of 2024 as well, saying a large proportion of the Ukrainian population had opposed joining NATO at the time.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz called on Russia to end its "dangerous provocations" after two Russian missiles and a jet-powered drone crashed in Poland on Friday.

Merz delivered those remarks after having met with NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte in Berlin on Monday.

"Poland can count on our full solidarity. And if necessary, NATO will of course defend every inch of allied territory," Merz said.

Merz said Europe and NATO must strengthen their defenses.

Drones have repeatedly strayed into NATO airspace in the year since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

The incident also came at a time as Poland was hosting a two-week military exercise by Ukraine's allies.

German startup investments in fields such as robotics and defense are set to almost triple this year, a study noted on Monday.

The German Start-up Association and the Joachim Herz Foundation study predicted that investments in so-called "deep tech startups" will surge from just €2.9 billion ($3.17 billion) last year to 8.1 billion ($8.9 billion) this year.

The study described the rise as a "major success for Germany as a business location."

"Deep tech" typically refers to developing cutting-edge technologies based on scientific research, such as AI, biotechnology and quantum computing.

A handful of massive fundraising rounds by firms including humanoid robot developer Neura Robotics,  AI drone maker Helsing and defense tech group Quantum Systems drove the investment boom.

The study also showed about 300 new deep tech startups are expected to be founded this year, a 40% rise compared with last year.

Newly found startups tend to be founded around economic hubs like Berlin and Hamburg, which are also home to leading universities and research institutes.

The study also highlighted challenges, including limited funding compared with their US counterparts and insufficient support to move startups from the laboratory to the real world.

Police in several locations across Germany reported large numbers of bomb threats targeting schools.

They said that while they were investigating the claims, they did not initially have reason to treat them as credible threats.

More than 400 schools in the southwestern state of Baden-Württemberg received threats, and more than 250 in Saxony-Anhalt received the emails, with several other regions also targeted on Monday morning.

Similar reports have also emerged to the north of Germany, in Denmark.

As in Germany, Danish police said they did not believe the threats were credible, "but they understandably create insecurity locally at the schools."

Read more about the disruptive incidents that have targeted Europe in recent weeks.

Germany's Freie Wähler (Free Voters) party have chosen a new chairman, weeks after their former front man Hubert Aiwanger unexpectedly passed away on November 4.

The party announced on Monday that Bavaria's Digital Affairs Fabian Mehring is to succeed Aiwanger both as party leader on the federal level and as one of two co-chairs of the Bavaria section of they party. The second state co-chair still needs to be decided.

Aiwanger was found dead in a Berlin hotel room at the age of 55 with no foul play suspected. He's been the party's defining figure for almost four decades, having led the Free Voters to substantial success, especially in Bavaria.

The Free Voters are originally a grass roots party in Bavaria and sit on the conservative edge of the political spectrum. They've been in government in Bavaria as junior coaltion partners of the Christian Social Union (CSU), sister party to Chancellor Merz's Christian Democratic Union (CDU).

There are also changes in the Bavarian state government. Tobias Gotthardt is to take over as economy minister, while Environment Minister Thorsten Glauber is set to become deputy premier behind Bavaria state Premier Markus Söder. The appointments still require formal approval by party conventions.

German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul has inisted that NATO was ready to defend itself in the face of potential Russian threats against any of its member states.

"We will always defend every inch of our NATO territory," Wadephul said at the NATO Parliamentary Assembly in Berlin.

His comments come after three Russian projectiles violated Polish airspace on Friday and crashed in the southeast of the country.

Wadephul is attending the NATO assembly in Berlin and DW has   a dedicated blog on those talks  where you can read all about how Russia's war in Ukraine is taking center stage for the defense alliance.

A massive strike is underway in Germany hitting major car brands another manufacturing factors. Metal and electrical workers are demanding better pay ahead of upcoming wage talks later this week. The strike has been initiated by IG Metall, Germany’s biggest and most powerful union.

Famous car brands Mercedes and BMW  were affected as was an Opel plant, which is part of the international Stellantis group.

The strikes began on Friday and are due to continue until Tuesday. Wage negotiations are then set to continue on Wednesday with another round of collective bargaining for some 3.7 million workers across the sector.

The union is demanding a pay rise of 5% over one year while the employers association, Gesamtmetall, has offered a one-time payment and a pay increase of 1.3%.

The tough struggle over wages comes as especially the German car industry is facing serious headwinds because of higher energy prices, US tariffs and mounting Chinese competition.

A German investigative media report published on Monday claims that Russia would be able to launch a nuclear-armed satellite, called Sputnik-S, into orbit within the space of about 60 days if it wished.

The report from public broadcasters WDR, NDR and the Süddeutsche Zeitung newspaper, cites a warning from German and other western intelligence agencies that it says was circulated at the start of November.

It said that a launch "could" take place by December, without quoting the document or clarifying whether it was talking only about a Russian capability, or a more firm intention.

The report said the satellite itself had been built several years ago and was being stored in the Moscow area.

German authorities did not respond to requests for comment on the record while the Russian Embassy in Berlin said the claims were part of a "propaganda" campaign.

The report matches longstanding warnings, mainly but not exclusively from the US, that Russia could be preparing a nuclear strike in Earth orbit designed to take out a large number of satellites.

This could have a severe impact on intelligence, communications, logisticts, navigation and other key services.

Russia's war in Ukraine, and the Ukrainian military's reliance on the Starlink satellite internet service, has provided an additional reminder of the strategic significance of satellites in orbit.

German exports to Africa have reached a new record. That’s according to a fresh study just as the country's president embarks on a trip to several African countries.

Exports are expected to rise by 6% in 2026 to reach about 30 billion euros ($33bn).

What’s behind the growing demand are especially orders from South Africa, Egypt, Tunisia, Nigeria, Angola and Kenya — countries where inflation has been dropping and exchange rates are more stable.

The biggest single export at the moment is a high-speed train network to Egypt. Other main exports include electrical equipment, optical instruments, plastics and pharmaceuticals, as well as food products, including dairy goods, cereals and baked goods.

The data is being reported by the Reuters news agency, based on the government-owned agency Germany Trade & Invest (GTAI), which promotes foreign trade and investment in Germany.

In 2025, exports to Africa had risen by 8% while in 2024 it had gone down.

The Germangovernment has blamed oil and gas-producing nations for the COP climate conference ending without an agreement.

"The oil and gas industry is still dragging its feet," German Environment Minister Carsten Schneider said after the UN climate talks had failed on Sunday. "Some oil-producing nations realize that the situation is becoming serious for them — that is why they are blocking it so vehemently," saidSchneider.

Almost two days into overtime, the COP31 climate talks in Turkey ended on Sunday as many countries, including the EU, rejected a final declaration.

Major sticking points at the summit included a commitment to accelerate global electrification and whether or not to explicitly mention plans to phase out fossil fuels. The suggested final declaration put forward by the COP presidency did not mention fossil fuels and according to critics would have undermined the shift away from fossil fuels.

"I understand that this poses a threat to the business model of those countries that sell us oil and gas. But electrification will make the world a more peaceful and stable place," Schneider said.

The inability to agree on a final declaration comes as climate change is increasingly linked to worsening heatwaves, floods and other natural catastrophes.

German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier begins a five-day trip to Africa that will take him to Ivory Coast, Ghana and Kenya with a focus on economic cooperation and the training of skilled workers.

He begins in Abidjan, where he is due to meet Ivorian President Alassane Ouattara. Steinmeier will also visit a vocational college and the International Academy for Counter-Terrorism before travelling on to Ghana.

In the capital Accra on Tuesday, he is set to open the German-African Business Summit, which according to its website, "brings together senior business executives, policymakers, investors, and industry leaders from across Germany and Africa."

His final stop will be Kenya, where he will meet President William Ruto in Nairobi on Wednesday.

The German president is traveling with a German business delegation and wants to encourage closer economic ties and greater investment in Africa.

The trip is his 11th to sub-Saharan Africa and his final one as president as his term in office due to end next March.

#393. Thanksgiving parade 2026: Macy’s Thanksgiving Parade new start time, streaming options

Thanksgiving is almost here, and for some folks, the most important part of the holiday isn't the food, family, or football. It's watching a bunch of big floats during a parade in New York City.

OK, maybe that's not literally true, but the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade is an annual touchstone for lots of folks, and it's almost here. As always, there are lots of things to know about it, such as when it starts, where you can watch it, and, this year especially, whether the weather will affect the parade as expected. Let's get into it.

First and foremost, the parade starts at 8:30 a.m. ET and runs until noon on Saturday. Yes, you read that right: The Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade is not actually on Thanksgiving Day this year. There are very good reasons for that, which we'll get to in a second.

It's worth noting that, unlike most other live televised events, it will not air simultaneously in every time zone. Instead, per NBC News, it will air from 8:30 to around noon in each time zone, so no matter where you are, turn the TV on at 8:30.

The parade will air on NBC, so if you have a TV that gets local channels via cable, an antenna, or another way to watch TV, just turn on NBC.

If you don't have any of those things, Peacock will work, too. I should note that you'll need at least Peacock Premium to stream your local NBC station, and there is no free trial for that. You'll either have to pay $12.99 per month or borrow someone else's login. The best tech deal this week The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile Products available for purchase through affiliate links. If you buy something through links on our site, Mashable may earn an affiliate commission.

The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile

According to NBC News, this year's parade will feature 100 inflatables in total, the most they've ever used for one of these. You can see the full balloon lineup on the Macy's website, but rest assured that all your favorites are likely included, like Sonic the Hedgehog and the Pink Panther. There are also new ones, like a DoorDash float and a GEICO float. One float will also act as a tribute of sorts for Fiona the hippo, which is nice.

Performers include Teddy Swims and Megan Moroney on the main stage, with other floats featuring acts such as the Baha Men, Blues Traveler, Icona Pop, and Devo. There's a little something for everyone.

And now for the bad news: There's a weather system moving up the East Coast that has caused the parade organizers to reschedule it this year, per NBC News.

Two storms combined into one in the American South, with the result expected to bring wind gusts of up to 45mph to New York City starting on Thursday morning. This is a problem because the city has an upper limit of 34mph for gusts regarding big inflatable objects. The parade was still scheduled for Thursday until the middle of Wednesday afternoon, when organizers and New York City officials decided to push it back to Saturday.

Unfortunately, that means you'll need a plan B for Thursday morning entertainment, but, more importantly, this should keep everyone who planned to attend the parade on Thursday safe.
