#384. The ‘True Crime Community’ Is Inspiring Violent Attacks Through TikTok

The fetishization of mass murderers has been around since long before TikTok.

Bonnie and Clyde were folk heroes. Serial killer Ted Bundy was adored by a legion of female fans. And the mother of Columbine shooter Dylan Klebold reported receiving love letters to her son in the mail written by young girls.

More recently, this phenomenon has manifested in a network known as the True Crime Community, or TCC, a group of mainly young people who lionize mass shooters like Klebold. (This group is distinct from true crime enthusiasts who like to read books or listen to podcasts about unsolved crimes.)

While this community has been around for years, in 2026, it moved en masse to TikTok. There, supercharged by the video-sharing platform's powerful black-box algorithm, the community’s violent, nihilistic worldview expanded its reach dramatically, serving up graphic content to users who had never been exposed before.

Tracking the scale and real-world impact of the network has been difficult, because the coded language, symbols, and memes used within the group are constantly changing to avoid detection by platforms and law enforcement. On TikTok some of the group members most interested in violence began referring to the group as the True Cringe Community. When TikTok blocked that term, they began referring to themselves as the True Larp Community.

But now, for the first time, the Network Contagion Research Institute (NCRI), a Princeton, New Jersey–based nonprofit that tracks online extremism, has collated data that shows that attacks and attempted attacks linked to the TCC have exploded by 200 percent over the last two years. The data, shared exclusively with WIRED ahead of publication, shows that the number of annual attacks or attempted attacks have gone from 13 reported in all of 2024 to 30 by mid-October this year.

The footprint of these attacks also expanded globally. Attacks and attempted attacks linked to the TCC were registered in 13 different countries in 2026, with two of every three incidents happening outside the US. And NCRI’s researchers predict that without intervention, the situation is about to get much worse.

“This is heading towards an explosion,” Joel Finkelstein, chief science officer with NCRI, tells WIRED. “That's what the data is suggesting, and the data is unambiguous. It's heading next year to a point where this is going to be happening more than once a week. That's really alarming.”

The TCC is part of a broader online nihilistic violent extremism movement and often overlaps with the extremist crime network known as “The Com,” which incorporates groups like 764 and No Lives Matter,

The TCC’s members, a large proportion of which are teenagers, share content online that references, glorifies, mimics, and simulates school shooters, mass shooters, and serial killers from all over the world. This is done through flattering videos posted on social media, taking pictures replicating the hand signals attackers used during their killing sprees, or wearing the T-shirts worn by mass shooters. The members also use AI to turn videos of mass shootings into cartoons or anime in order to avoid detection by online platforms’ trust and safety teams.

Beyond posting fan fiction about their favorite school shooters, this community also encourages others to carry out their own attacks. If successful, those attackers in turn become part of TCC’s ever-expanding lore and mythology, becoming part of a self-reinforcing cycle.

While writing its report, NCRI researchers documented numerous other attacks linked to the group, including the September 18 shooting at a high school in the Philippines and an October 1 attack at a secondary school in Torreón, Mexico. There was also a shooting on October 12 at a middle school in France and a knife attack on October 13 in South Africa that have also been linked to the TCC community.

While TCC was found on a lot of platforms online, for the first 10 years of its existence, much of its activity was centered on Tumblr. But in January, the site implemented a ban wave that drove much of the community to TikTok, where the platform’s unique algorithm put TCC-related content in front of a much broader audience, according to a report from the Institute of Strategic Dialogue published earlier this month.

“Algorithmically driven engagement has supercharged its spread,” the report’s authors wrote. “Unlike Tumblr, where the fandom is largely isolated, TikTok actively works to expose users to new content through its algorithm, resulting in TCC videos being served to a much larger audience.”

Finkelstein says that while TikTok does remove some of the accounts his team flags to the platform, in general the company is not doing enough to combat the problem.

“[TikTok’s] capacity to manage this is very spotty,” Finkelstein said. “This is an uncontained open wound. Whatever measures they think they're making to manage this are obviously inadequate to deal with the damage that the community is unleashing. If you took TikTok offline for a few weeks, my guess is these attacks would slow down because there's not a permission structure in place that's encouraging vulnerable youth to go out and murder people in order to be famous with their peers because they're so depressed and living in their mom's basement and spending 10 hours a day on social media.”

TikTok, whose US operations are now owned primarily by a group of investors including Oracle, controlled by GOP megadonor and Donald Trump ally Larry Ellison, said it had rules in place to proactively remove TCC-linked content.

“We enforce strict rules against content that promotes violence or glorifies perpetrators of mass violence, and we had already banned a large number of the accounts in this report,” a TikTok spokesperson tells WIRED.

WIRED shared the report with several other researchers who closely track TCC activity online, and all broadly concluded that NCRI’s assessment was accurate. One independent researcher, Ry Terran, pointed out that accurately tracking this movement is difficult given the dense nature of the language they use around attacks.

“When examining perpetrators' social media, I see that they frequently frame threats as a joke, a LARP, or AI-generated,” Terran tells WIRED. “Social media companies should not take these claims at face value, but rather report any credible threats. Without appropriate interventions, TCC-inspired attacks will likely continue to increase.”

Another European-based researcher, who requested anonymity due to fears of retaliation, tells WIRED, “We're panicking here in Europe.” The researcher collaborates with European law enforcement agencies and says they are concerned about the increasing number of attacks taking place globally.

Finkelstein says that US lawmakers and law enforcement need to do more in order to combat this problem. “The FBI seems to want to deal with it by arresting kids. None of this makes any sense,” he says. “We've got to step back and see the scale of this. We should be turning to our law enforcement agencies and our national security apparatus that has the ear of the president and say something's got to be done about this.”

The FBI declined to comment, and the White House did not respond to a request for comment. The Department of Homeland Security referred WIRED to the FBI.

“The Justice Department remains vigilant against the threat of such violent extremist networks that operate within the United States and around the globe,” Wyn Hornbuckle, a spokesman for the Department of Justice, tells WIRED.

Update: 11/25/2026, 9:02 AM EDT: WIRED has updated a reference to the Network Contagion Research Institute.

#383. Apple Watch Series 12 review: Same design, better health tracking, and more listening in

Looks are deceiving for the new Apple Watch Series 12. On the outside, it appears to be the exact same smartwatch as last year (...and the year before that). But on the inside, it packs redesigned heart rate sensors and a faster S11 chip that enables intriguing new health-tracking features and AI tools, including the Siri AI beta.

After wearing the Series 12 for the past three-ish weeks, I'm pleased to report that some of these invisible upgrades make a pretty meaningful difference — and that they don't chip away at the watch's battery life. My testing found that the Series 12 lasts slightly longer than the Series 11 from fall 2025.

That said, I wouldn't miss half of the new AI-powered "Audio Intelligence" tools if Apple suddenly Thanos-snapped them out of existence. Always-on AI notetakers like Plaud, Pocket, and Bee are a growing trend in Silicon Valley, but they're not for me.

The Series 12's external changes are primarily cosmetic. Apple added a ceramic case option to the mix again, giving buyers a new premium alternative to its aluminum and titanium variants (which now come in new shades like dark bronze and radiant gold). There are some fresh band styles and materials to chew over, too. For testing, Apple sent me a Series 12 with a light gold aluminum case and a sand Sport Band. I'm more of a silver girl myself, but it's very pretty.

Each case type is available in 42mm or 46mm sizes, as usual. They're priced as follows:

Aluminum case: Starting at $399 with optional cellular connectivity ($100 extra)

Titanium case: Starting at $699 with cellular connectivity

Ceramic case: Starting at $899 with cellular connectivity

All of the Series 12's case options are still waterproof for up to 50 meters and carry an IP6X dust resistance rating, but Apple says the glass on the aluminum Series 12 is more durable than before. Otherwise, it's identical to the Series 11 (which was basically identical to the Series 10).

Longtime Apple Watch users who are holding out for an exciting redesign might just stop reading here, understandably. If it's any consolation, we might get one next year. But as someone new to the wearable space, I will say this is a very attractive and comfortable watch. Familiarity breeds contempt, as St. Augustine or Taylor Swift or whomever once said.

Located on the underside of its base, the Series 12's new "Health Sensing System" is a cluster of advanced optical and electrical heart sensors. It has more electrodes that cover a larger surface area for better skin contact during ECG readings, rearranged photodiodes that are better at picking up light, and bigger, more efficient green LEDs that take readings way more frequently.

While older Apple Watches only logged the user's heart rate continuously during workouts and every five minutes otherwise, the Series 12 now measures heart rate every five seconds throughout the day, no matter what you're doing. As proof, these near-real-time readings are available at a glance on a new heart rate watch face widget, or "complication."

The Series 12's fancier sensors also up the frequency of its heart rate variability readings from every two hours to every five minutes. (HRV is a key stress indicator.)

These changes make the Series 12's heart rate data much more precise and detailed than before, and more useful for non-athletes. In turn, other features that use this data should be more accurate, too — Vitals and the Exercise ring, to name a couple. I think this will be the Series 12's biggest selling point for most people.

Apple reworked its pedometer model for the Series 12 to track steps more accurately when your arms are still. It also added a step count complication, aptly called "Steps." That one might not seem like a huge deal, but it actually resolves a common pain point with older Apple Watches: Users previously had to DIY a step-count complication by installing a separate pedometer app. It's great to see.

The Series 12 can now produce a "Readiness" score, a 0 to 10 rating of your capacity for physical activity based on your recent exercise, sleep habits, and Vitals. It needs a week of data before it starts working, FYI. The best tech deal this week The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile

The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile

I like that this score adjusts throughout the day — it's not a one-and-done daily reading. One of my mornings started at a 6 ("Ready") after a decent night's sleep. By the evening that same day, it had fallen to a 4 ("Pace Yourself") because I went on a long, brisk afternoon walk.

That said, the feature mostly tells me what I could already figure out on my own. I don't necessarily need a score to know I'm less inclined to work out right after exercising. Athletes with more varied training regimens will probably get more value out of this feature than the average person.

Music Recognition with Shazam now works automatically. It usually takes only a couple of seconds to identify a song, depending on the amount of background noise, and it's always spot-on.

Sound Recognition can alert you to sounds such as sirens, doorbells, smoke alarms, barking dogs, and car horns. It liked to confuse a train's "door closing" chime for an appliance bell, but was otherwise accurate in my testing. It's a useful addition for people who are deaf and hard of hearing.

Live Rewind transcribes the tail end of a recent conversation when you double-press the Series 12's dial (aka "Digital Crown"). Apple says it can show the last 15 seconds of speech, but in practice it's closer to 10 seconds. Either way, it feels kind of pointless. It's such a short window of time that you might as well just ask the person you're chatting with to repeat themselves. It's also not correct 100 percent of the time. It once confused the phrase "pencil me in" for "Pennsylvania."

Finally, there's Siri Recap, which is essentially a built-in AI notetaker. (It's meant for oral conversations, but it's also summarized TikToks I've watched and phone calls I've taken on speaker mode.) Its outlines are pretty macro and vary in their helpfulness depending on the conversation. I found it really good for recapping food orders and reviewing topics discussed in my Italian classes, but a little clunky when it comes to casual conversations. It doesn't distinguish between different speakers and sometimes mashes topics together. It's also not completely accurate — it said a friend named their baby "Popsicle" (no <3) — but it seems to be improving as I've continued to use it.

I struggle with Siri Recap the most because it makes me feel like a creep. It doesn't alert you when it's listening in on a conversation, much less the person(s) you're speaking with, so it's on you to tell them that you're documenting your private discussions for later reference. (Awkward!) Keep in mind that such admissions will likely change the nature of your interactions: People edit themselves and put up their guards when they know they're being watched.

Apple rated the Series 12 for up to 24 hours of battery life, but in my testing, it's offered around 45 to 51 hours of normal use per charge. (Crucially, I haven't needed to activate Low Power Mode to hit those numbers.) This is a real testament to the S11 chip's power efficiency. It's also a nice bump from the Series 11, which Mashable's Stan Schroeder described as "a one-and-a-half-day smartwatch."

Apple says the Series 12 charges faster than its predecessor, too. I don't have a Series 11 handy to verify that, but I've been impressed with the Series 12's charging speed. Right before going to bed one night, I realized it didn't have enough charge for sleep tracking, which requires at least 30 percent battery. Luckily, just five minutes on an outlet bumped it from 23 to 39 percent battery.

With its latest mainstream smartwatch, Apple refines a familiar design with near-live heart rate tracking, noticeable battery-life gains, and a step-tracking widget — a small but welcome quality-of-life tweak. Audio Intelligence, meanwhile, takes a back seat to these more meaningful improvements.

For most people, the Series 12 is the best Apple Watch to buy right now (unless, of course, you're willing to wait for next year's redesign). It's an easy recommendation over the more expensive Apple Watch Ultra 4, which offers much of the same functionality but adds longer battery life and enhanced durability for outdoor and endurance activities. Compared to the budget-friendly Apple Watch SE 3, the Series 12 is also a more future-proof choice, with a considerably more comprehensive suite of health and fitness tracking features to boot.

#382. Gap names new Athleta CEO, says Old Navy turnaround is seeing signs of progress

Gap Inc. on Thursday announced Ashley Kechter will be the next president and CEO of its Athleta brand, effective Dec. 14.

The retailer also said Old Navy's turnaround is showing signs of progress, sending shares up more than 11% Friday.

Kechter comes to Gap from activewear retailer Vuori, where she was global president and oversaw the brand's global business strategy, marketing and financials. She was previously global brand president of Fabletics and began her career at Gap before that.

"I'm excited to return to Gap Inc. and partner with [Gap CEO Richard Dickson] and the team to strengthen our connection with customers and shape the brand's next chapter," Kechter said in a statement.

The announcement comes after Lululemon poached former Athleta CEO Maggie Gauger to be its chief product officer last month.

"Clearly, we're disappointed with Athleta's performance, and we recognize there's a lot of work ahead," Dickson told CNBC. "We had been in rebuild mode, but now we're really in turnaround mode."

Dickson said the company is focused on getting back to its fundamentals: fabrications, feature, form, function and fit. Dickson added that Kechter will be conducting a "comprehensive review" of the brand to reposition Athleta for future success.

While the execution of its strategy has thus far "fallen short," Dickson said this new approach will allow Athleta to fully realize its potential.

Gap also reported mixed fiscal third-quarter earnings on Thursday and posted flat overall comparable sales. Wall Street had been expecting a comparable sales increase of 1.3%, according to StreetAccount.

Net sales grew 2%, though demand softened in October and early November due to warmer weather, the company said. Store sales increased 1%, while online sales increased 3%.

Gap also said it's recorded a $420 million adjustment to cost of goods sold and a $21 million adjustment to interest income from tariff refunds so far this year.

The company lowered its full-year net sales outlook to be "roughly flat," down from previous guidance of up between 1% and 1.5%. Gap is also now expecting adjusted earnings per share of between $2.29 and $2.34, down from an earlier expectation of between $2.35 and $2.45 per share.

Dickson said in an interview that much of the lowered guidance was due to warmer weather in the first two weeks of the quarter, but he said Gap is expecting "meaningful acceleration" in shopping ahead of the peak holiday season.

"We're monitoring the trends, and we're going to remain agile as we respond to the changing business trends," Dickson said.

Here's how the company performed in its fiscal third quarter compared with what Wall Street was expecting, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG:

For the quarter, Gap reported net income of $311 million, or 86 cents per share, compared with $236 million, or 62 cents per share, the year prior. Sales rose slightly from $3.94 billion the year prior.

At Athleta, net sales were down 14% compared with last year, coming in at $220 million. Comparable sales for the banner sank 15%, which the company attributed to "limited traction" from efforts to modernize its merchandise and marketing. `

The company's namesake brand saw 9% comparable sales growth for the quarter, with net sales of $1.1 billion, marking an 11% increase compared with last year. Dickson said it was the brand's 12th consecutive quarter of positive comparable sales.

"Gap is really firing on all cylinders, and the consistency of the brand is really giving us confidence in the brand's ability to continue its momentum," Dickson said.

The Old Navy banner saw flat comparable sales for the quarter and net sales of $2.3 billion, up 1% compared with last year. It's the first earnings report since the brand, which has been experiencing sluggish sales, named Michael Francis as its new CEO last quarter. Francis began his role at Old Navy on Nov. 2.

Banana Republic saw its net sales sink 3% compared with last year, which the company attributed to delayed demand for cold-weather categories and a women's fall assortment that fell flat. Wall Street had been expecting growth of 1.5%, according to StreetAccount.

Dickson said the brand has since introduced new products and seen demand "rebound" as cooler weather has set in across the country.

"We've been encouraged by the early customer response, and we should see sequential improvement in the fourth quarter," he said. "There's some work to do here, but with peak selling still ahead, I'm confident that the team is focused on the right areas and [will] ultimately position Banana well for growth."

#381. Rembrandt's 'The Night Watch' is more alive than you'd expect

A new project and exhibition, "The Night Watch Lives," lifts the veil on the hidden world of microbes covering one of the most famous paintings of the Dutch Golden Age.

Rembrandt van Rijn's "The Night Watch" is one of the most famous paintings of the Dutch Golden Age. Amsterdam's Rijksmuseum, where the work is on display, hails the artist's 1642 masterpiece as "the turning point in his career and as the superlative example of his creative genius."

In the painting, Rembrandt made dramatic use of light and shadow to guide the viewer's eye to key figures. And unlike static group portraits typical of his era, the artist depicted Amsterdam's civic guards in mid-action, as they prepare to march out.

Beyond the sense of movement featured in "The Night Watch," the painting itself is also alive in a way that's rarely taken into consideration — through the microscopic organisms living on the canvas.

The research project "The Night Watch Lives" explores exactly that question: What kinds of life forms inhabit the surface of the famous painting?

The study is a collaborative scientific and exhibition project between the Rijksmuseum and ARTIS-Micropia — an Amsterdam museum dedicated to the world of microorganisms.

It's part of the broader "Operation Night Watch" restoration and research project described as the "biggest and most wide-ranging ever study and restoration of Rembrandt's most famous painting," started in 2019. Conservators and scientists in this project have been examining every aspect of Rembrandt's masterpiece using cutting-edge technology, seeking new insights into its materials, condition and history — and now, its microbiome.

The idea behind "The Night Watch Lives" was to "put microbes in a positive spotlight," Eline van Bloois, who led the research, told DW. "Honestly, if you're asking me — I'm a microbiologist, so I'm biased of course — but they really deserve more positive attention."

Over a period of six months, van Bloois will be taking samples once a month directly from the famous painting at the Rijksmuseum, accompanied by the people working on the restoration of "The Night Watch."

Using small sterile discs gently pressed against selected areas of the painting, the samples collect microscopic material from both varnished and unvarnished sections.

These samples are then cultivated in laboratories, allowing previously invisible microbes to grow into visible colonies that can be studied and identified.

At the "The Night Watch Lives" exhibition, visitors can view Petri dishes containing the cultivated microbial colonies. A life-size reproduction of Rembrandt's masterpiece also shows where the samples were taken, and which microorganisms were found there.

At the exhibition's opening on November 11, the installation included the findings of two of van Bloois' sampling sessions. Four more will be added over the coming months, allowing the museum's visitors to follow the results of the study as it unfolds.

That means the exhibition's visitors "will be figuring out what I've found as I'm figuring it out myself," explains the microbiologist. "We really take them through that journey with us."

People often fear microbes or associate them with disease, even though the vast majority of these microscopic organisms are actually harmless or vital to human survival.

Some of the organisms found on the painting "are very commonly found on human skin, for instance, and they're a healthy part of the microbiome; most humans actually have these bacteria with them," says van Bloois, adding that the presence of these microbes on the painting made sense, since humans are often near the work.

But another bacterium stood out in the samples: Microbacterium saccharophilum, a species first identified at a sugar refinery in Japan in 2013.  How this microorganism ended up on the Dutch "Night Watch," or when, is a guessing game.

"It's part of the fun and part of the frustration in microbiology. You cannot ask the microbes where they originate from," says van Bloois. "It would make our lives a bit easier, but it's also fun to have a little bit of a mystery."

The samples also revealed bacteria from soil, often found in plant roots. Could these organisms somehow harm the painting? Could plants start growing on the work?

Van Bloois explains why this is highly unlikely: On the painting, the bacteria can form inactive spores, but for the study, the researcher "provided them with all the nutrients and the right temperature and the right humidity that allowed them to grow again."

Still, studying these organisms may eventually contribute to understanding how paintings age, how environmental conditions affect cultural heritage, and how museums can better preserve priceless works of art.

As to whether the microorganisms could date back to Rembrandt's time, the microbiologist says that's also "highly unlikely" — but here again, microbes cannot reveal their origin story.

As part of the larger "Operation Night Watch" team, van Bloois is definitely inspired by this "group effort where everyone is just really enthusiastic about telling these stories and adding to the knowledge surrounding 'The Night Watch.'"

The microbiological samples revealed by the laboratory process resemble abstract art in miniature: colorful clusters, delicate textures and intricate patterns created by living organisms.

And as the study is unfolding publicly, it also feels like an artistic performance of its own.

The project also perfectly embodies the full name of the museum where the exhibition is held: Natura Artis Magistra, a Latin phrase that translates to "nature is the teacher of art and science," as the microbiologist points out: "It's really cool to see science and art all come together in this project."

The exhibition "The Night Watch Lives" runs at ARTIS-Micropia in Amsterdam until the end of May 2027.

#379. Airplane Turbulence Is Extremely Hard to Predict, but Maybe Not for Long

In the early 1500s, an Italian polymath named Leonardo da Vinci took a good crack at exactly the phenomenon that makes nervous fliers clutch their airplane seats in fear and flight attendants push their carts back to the galleys with haste: turbulence.

Da Vinci was fascinated by swirling, chaotic eddies of water, movements so complex that he made hundreds of drawings of his observations. Why, exactly, did water—any fluid, really, be it atmospheric air or blood in the heart—move in that way?

Now the world has ChatGPT and self-driving cars and solar farms, and it still doesn’t exactly know how turbulence works. “It’s the hardest remaining problem in classical physics, and it’s one we need to fly through,” says Michael Murillo, a professor of theoretical and computational physics at Michigan State University.

Now a bumper crop of data-driven efforts to predict and avoid turbulence could get fliers closer to a smooth flight. Twenty terabytes of data are created by an airplane’s engine in one hour of commercial flying, according to the International Air Transport Association, with more broadcast by airplanes midflight: GPS position, altitude, speed. An “electronic flight bag,” basically a specialized iPad, is equipped with navigation charts and manuals and can transmit its own information, as long as the airplane’s internet connection cooperates. Satellites watch and collect it all.

“Air traffic has gone up, and communication costs and the costs of putting computers on aircraft have come down,” says Larry Cornman, a physicist with the National Science Foundation’s National Center for Atmospheric Research who has been studying turbulence for decades. “The time is now to work on these things because we can do them.”

This is good news for aviation safety. More than 200 people were seriously injured on US airplanes in turbulence-related incidents between 2009 and 2023, according to FAA data. Turbulence is also getting worse. Climate change alters the atmospheric conditions around the world’s jet streams, creating destabilizing wind shear. From the cockpit of an airplane, this translates into sudden, clear-air turbulence, difficult to see or predict. Historically, pilots’ only method of avoiding turbulence is heeding the warning of those who accidentally went through it before them, and hoping that nothing had changed.

But just in the past two years, Cornman’s decades of work on turbulence has been put into the field in ways it couldn’t be before, part of several projects coordinated by the US federal government and the airline industry. One breakthrough came when Cornman and an FAA air traffic controller determined that aircrafts’ federally required broadcasts of their positions, altitude, and speed could be used to spot unexpected turbulence, without requiring new hardware or software onboard. Researchers can use this crowdsourced, public data to make predictions about when and where turbulence will pop up.

In September, the National Science Foundation announced a $30 million award to nine universities to stand up a new center dedicated to predicting turbulence—in the air, but also in the charged particles inside a fusion reactor, and in the gas clouds that stretch across space.

“Turbulence is the reason we don’t have fusion energy yet,” says Murillo, who heads up the new center, called Transformative Explorations in Multi-Physics and Engineering of Scientific Turbulence, or Tempest. The chaotic swirling of superhot plasma inside a reactor allows heat to leak out, preventing the material from reaching the temperatures needed to allow nuclei to fuse. The US federal government wants to get closer to figuring that out.

“Closer,” because turbulence is impossible to perfectly predict, scientists say. For one thing, turbulence occurs at many different, small scales at the same time. Air swirling around an airplane breaks into eddies, then smaller eddies, and then even smaller eddies, with each interacting with each other—too many variables, happening too quickly, to mathematically account for. For another, tiny changes—wind speed, temperature—can eventually dramatically alter air movement, suddenly altering the turbulence once predicted. To make perfect forecasts, one would need a perfect picture of exactly what’s going on in the atmosphere at all times.

But increasing sophisticated applications of machine learning could allow scientists to get closer to knowing what’s going to happen when, says Murillo. And while brute, computational force can’t solve the turbulence problem, AI agents might give the effort a boost. OpenAI’s blockbuster announcement this fall that it had resolved the Navier-Stokes problem—equations that are the beginning of all turbulence models—suggests LLMs could help.

“Turbulence has been a problem only human minds could work on; as of this year, that's no longer true,” says Murillo.

To make flying better, the aviation industry doesn’t necessarily need to solve turbulence. It needs to get better at knowing what sort of conditions create it and not send airplanes there.

One company in Tel Aviv, SkyPath, uses those in-plane iPads and their accelerometers to collect and share crowdsourced data between different airplanes, even if they don’t fly for the same airline. (This sort of dating sharing can be a sensitive topic for competing companies; SkyPath says it assuages these concerns by ensuring that data is anonymized before it’s shared.) More than 40,000 of these devices have SkyPath installed on them, says CEO Maya Shpak; the company says that several major airlines, including American, use the technology. SkyPath combines that collected data with additional information, including weather forecasts, and uses machine intelligence to make predictions about the future state of the air. The app helps pilots avoid turbulent air and warn passengers and crew members that choppiness is coming, 10 to 15 minutes before it happens.

One pilot named Eric who uses SkyPath, who asked WIRED not to use his full name because he was not authorized to speak to the media, said the app is a helpful tool that allows him to warn passengers what to expect. His issue is the same as those studying turbulence: One can’t take measurements everywhere all at once.

“It’s like any crowdsourced software,” says the pilot. “It only works if everyone uses it, and no one wants to use it until everyone else is.” Today, several large operators are using the app, which makes it especially useful in areas with lots of flights, he says.

Cornman, the physicist, wants to keep all these advances in perspective. “No matter what people say, we’re not getting close to 100 percent, 90 percent, 80 percent [predictive accuracy] anytime soon,” he says. “It’s too complicated a problem.” Smoother skies, if not perfect ones, are ahead.

#378. This boiled bag of offal is banned in the US. In Scotland it's a fine-dining treat

Anthony Bourdain loved haggis. But even the late, great American chef, writer and television host recognized that Scotland’s national dish, with its “sinister sheep parts” wrapped in a shroud of mystery and half-invented history, could be a hard sell.

“Don’t let them tell you otherwise, that’s really one of life’s great pleasures,” Bourdain said on one of his gastro-curious pilgrimages to Glasgow. “There is no more unfairly reviled food on Earth than the haggis.”

A mash-up of diced lung, liver and heart mixed with oatmeal, beef suet, onion and assorted spices, haggis was traditionally made by stuffing these raw ingredients into the stomach of a recently slain sheep and boiling the lot to a state of palatability.

Instagrammable is not the word that immediately comes to mind. In our 21st-century world, where “clean” eating and processed pap overlap, haggis can seem like an “Outlander”-style outlier from another age.

Yet, by some alchemy, once cooked to its required “warm-reekin’ (steaming)” state, it adds up to much more than the sum of its modest parts. It’s offaly charm has kept nose-to-tail eating alive among a younger generation of Scots that has largely turned its back on the tripe, liver and kidneys their predecessors enjoyed (or endured).

Carefully prepared, haggis tastes both oaty and meaty; it is dark and crumbly, a little crispy at the edges but still moist; earthy but also savory and spicy; deep-tasting and profoundly warming, the perfect foil for its traditional garnish of floury mashed potatoes and orange bashed turnip.

“It’s like a cuddle for the stomach,” says Nicola Turner, a 35-year-old office administrator from Helensburgh, a town on western Scotland’s Firth of Clyde.

For children of the 1960s and ’70s, like crime novelist Ian Rankin, haggis meals were a choice between the classic meat-and-two-veg plate and the battered and deep-fried, chip-shop iteration loved by both his friend Bourdain and his quintessentially Scottish detective character, Inspector John Rebus.

Now myriad other treatments have blossomed.

“I’m pretty sure the first time I dined with AB in Edinburgh we had haggis in filo pastry with a jam-style – maybe blackcurrant – sauce,” Rankin recalled. “He was a big fan of haggis and of chip shops. Rebus will have enjoyed the occasional haggis supper from his local chip shop. He was definitely a fan, as am I.”

“It is all about the spicing and the texture,” says the Scottish food writer, novelist and cook Sue Lawrence, a champion of haggis’ adaptability for use in other dishes. “If you didn’t know what was in it, you wouldn’t think ‘oh that tastes of liver or whatever.’ It is all nicely chopped up and the oatmeal gives it a lovely texture. It could easily be a nice, big mince dish.”

These US restaurants and chefs are James Beard Award finalists

Lawrence uses haggis as an alternative to beef and pork ragù in lasagna and in her pastilla, a version of the North African dish in which a hand-made haggis from the Isle of Mull substitutes for the traditional poultry or seafood filling. The filo pastry savory is flavored with the spice blend ras el hanout, apricots, chile, orange zest and almonds before being sprinkled with cinnamon and icing sugar.

Such cultural crossovers serve as a reminder that haggis could easily be a dish with nothing specifically Scottish about it at all. Records of similar quick and portable preparations of the fast-perishing innards of sheep and other animals date back to ancient Rome and Greece.

Haggis-like combinations of offal and grains are part of the culinary history of several countries. Spain has chireta, Romania drob and Sweden polsa, while chaudin, or ponce, is a rice and meat-stuffed pig stomach that is a staple of Cajun cooking.

In neighboring England, recipes for “hagese,” “hagws of a schepe,” “haggas” or “haggus” pop up in recipe books published between the 15th and 17th centuries, probably preceding written records north of the border.

Etymological evidence points to the term “haggis” having its roots in Old Norse, suggesting an early version of an oat-and-offal sausage might have arrived in Britain and Ireland on a Viking longboat.

But ever since it was first optioned by the poet Robert Burns in the late 1700s, the haggis backstory has been monopolized by Scotland and the Scots, sometimes mischievously.

It is, according to the kind of lore that Burns engendered, the dish a doughty Highlander would carry with him as he drove cattle through the glens to the markets of the central belt or the perfect picnic for a whisky smuggler plying his illicit trade by moonlight.

From such romantic notions it was a short step to turning the haggis into a wee wild beastie, one with longer legs on one side that was thus condemned to run round and round whichever hill it lived on. In 2003, a poll of American tourists in Scotland found that one in three of them believed they might encounter such a confused creature on a Caledonian vacation.

Bourdain, a native New Yorker, may have qualified as haggis’ biggest admirer since Burns, but his compatriots at the US Department of Agriculture remain unconverted to offal-filled paunch. Haggis imports into the United States were prohibited in 1971 as part of a ban on the consumption of all livestock lungs. Authentic versions of old school haggis remain culinary contraband in the US, as hard to lay your hands on as Cuban cigars.

Across the rest of the world, it’s a different story. According to leading producer Simon Howie, haggis is more widely appreciated and consumed now than it has been since Burns improvised his “Address to a Haggis” for the entertainment of well-to-do Edinburgh acquaintances.

Firmly tongue-in-cheek, the poem lauds the “Great chieftain o’ the pudding race,” as exactly the kind of unpretentious, hearty fare required to nourish a nation of braveheart warriors.

In comparison to the enfeebling foreign muck enjoyed by the capital’s claret-quaffing elites of the time – the olio, fricassée or ragoût that would “sicken a sow” – Burns urges his readers to wonder at the magical impact of haggis on his fellow sons of Scotland’s soil.

As the English translation of the original Scots language version puts it:

These days synthetic casings have largely replaced stomach but ovine and porcine innards remain at the core of most of the haggis produced in its homeland, said Howie, who estimates that his company Simon Howie Butchers, accounts for around 60% of the roughly two million haggises produced every year.

For Howie, versatility, value for money and convenience explain why this staple of the Scottish larder is thriving. Typically haggis retails in Scotland, which accounts for half of global consumption by volume, for around £6, or $7.70 per kilogram ($3.36/pound). That’s around half the price of less expensive cuts of beef or a third of the price of Scotch lamb while enjoying a fairly similar nutritional and calorific profile.

“You can give your kids a meal that is not full of things you don’t want to feed them – for a few pounds you can feed three strapping lads,” Howie said.

“From a kitchen perspective, it is very simple because when it leaves our factory it is already cooked. So when you or a restaurant owner gets it into the kitchen all you have to do is heat it up to be piping hot. It couldn’t be more basic: a student with no cooking skills or a Michelin-starred chef do exactly the same thing to put it out on the plate.”

Its texture means haggis can also be usefully deployed in fine dining alongside leaner meat like venison or as a stuffing for poultry and game birds. Its spicy intensity means it is also finding uses in canapés and as a crouton-borne garnish for soups.

Buoyant sales are also underpinned by the increasing consumption of haggis in forms inspired by Scotland’s ethnic minorities.

Glasgow’s Sikh community pioneered haggis pakora in the 1990s and samosas, spring rolls and quesadillas have followed in its wake, often using a vegetarian version of the protein in which the offal is replaced by a mix of vegetables, pulses and mushrooms.

Such dishes are more than culinary twists. They are badges of belonging, and an indication that, two centuries after Burns grabbed it for the nation, haggis is as intimately entwined with Scots identity as ever.

Just ask Ross O’Cinneide, a promising 14-year-old fly-half in the junior section of Stirling County rugby club.

“Most of my friends and I like haggis,” he says. “Mum makes it for us sometimes after rugby and it’s got a very nice warming feeling. And it’s nice because it’s purely Scottish.”

#376. The Best TVs We’ve Tested (2026): Samsung, LG, TCL, Sony, and More.

Buying a new TV is always a big decision, namely because its a big piece of tech with a permanent place in your home that you'll be staring at for hours on end. Not to mention, some of the best of the best cost thousands of dollars. It doesn't help that most TVs look exactly the same and have nondescript names like the Samsung S95H—not great for narrowing your options.

Fear not. After stress-testing multiple TVs this year, I can attest to one simple truth: in 2026, you have more great options than ever. Art TVs and RGB TVs exploded onto the market and made the typical “just buy an OLED TV” advice seem like an ancient relic of a bygone. These top-performing televisions are my “desert island” picks, if said island had a power generator and good popcorn.

For more audio and home theater recommendations, check out related guides to the best OLED TVs, the best art TVs, the best RGB TVs, the best home theater projectors, and the best soundbars. If you truly don't know where to start, try our guide on how to buy a TV.

Update November 2026: We've revamped this entire guide, replacing nearly all of our top picks, Honorable Mentions, and Other TVs We've Tested.

The great debate: which size television is best for your living room? Does it even matter? The first thing to consider is price: an 80-inch TV is going to cost significantly more than a 65-inch one. In some cases, that means an extra grand or two for the privilege of seeing the stubble on Spider-Man’s face in great detail. Broadly speaking, the larger the room, the more useful a large screen is. The most popular size is 65 inches, which is a great option for most medium sizes spaces.

I’m partial to art televisions for one simple reason: They are useful even when they are turned off. Art TVs use an antireflective layer on top of the screen to create more realistic, textured still images like artwork or paintings. The best ones can replace a picture frame or wall art in any room, and double as great TVs.

TV tech has evolved in 2026, and the new kid on the block is RGB TVs. These new models shine red, blue, and green light through an LCD panel to create brighter, more vibrant color. OLED on the other hand can control the color of individual pixels and even turn them off completely, leading to excellent contrast and black levels.

Which one performs the best? That depends. RGB models like the LG Micro RGB Evo provide more control over picture quality, brightness, and contrast. OLED televisions like the Samsung S95H tend to look better on movie night, especially for nighttime scenes when inky blacks need to look realistic. If pressed, I’d pick an RGB TV model because you get more control over color, but that's just me.

I picked Samsung's The Frame Pro (2026) as the best overall TV because it has stunningly good picture quality and looks incredible showcasing a masterpiece painting on your wall. I remember staring at the 65-inch model on the wall of my office for two months, just marveling at high-res shipwreck photos and the real wood bezels that encompass the screen (and snap easily into place, by the way). With just about every painting, The Frame Pro showed intricate and detailed textures, as though you could reach out and feel the waves of an ocean or curve of a face.

The Frame Pro is also an excellent choice for movies and shows. Because of the anti-glare screen and matte finish, the dark corridors of scenes in The Batman on HBO had extra depth and animated movies like Toy Story 5 on Disney+ popped with color. Sure, it doesn't have the true black pixels of an OLED screen, but its other capabilities more than make up for it.

Extra features included easy-to-install stands (no screws needed) and a breakout box called the Samsung Wireless One Connect that lets you connect streaming devices and a game console from across the room. That means fewer wires dangling on the wall.

TCL is a more budget-focused television maker that tends to undercut the price of brands like Samsung and LG. A good example of this is the TCL QM7L Mini-LED TV above, which has a budget-friendly price but anything but oriented picture quality. If anything, this QLED model competes with some OLED TVs for inky, deep blacks and rich color. Will you notice any contrast issues when you watch the latest Pixar film? Probably not, especially since the QM7L also looked exceptionally bright in our tests.

A few other extras to mention: We loved the backlit remote, which makes it easier to punch up the volume or adjust picture quality settings in a dark room. You might even be able to skip a soundbar with this TV—the internal Bang & Olufsen speakers sound nice and loud.

Samsung, TCL, Hisense, and Sony released new RGB TVs this year, but it's the LG Micro RGB Evo that takes the crown, namely because you can tweak so many of its picture settings. In my tests,I could tweak the picture so much that movies and shows that mostly take place at night still looked visible, clear, and realistic. As one example among many, I remember tweaking settings for the movie Awake, a largely dark film, to the point where it looked clear and colorful. Other RGB models from Hisense and even Samsung struggled with those same dark scenes, no matter which setting I used.

Another major plus is that this model supports 100 percent of the color gamut specs for BT.2020, DCI-P3, and Adobe RGB. In layman's terms, if you watch a movie like Guardians of the Galaxy Vol. 2 (which also matches those specs), you will see a true rainbow of every color available, with unmatched color vibrancy. This TV is so striking that I came away thinking that OLED TVs are no longer the obvious gold standard in 2026.

Samsung made a big change to their flagship OLED model this year, the Samsung S95H. They ditch the Samsung One Connect breakout box that was required with previous models (and is still required on TVs like The Frame Pro). The TV now has ports directly on the panel, where you can connect video game consoles, streaming devices, or Blu-ray players directly. While that might create more cable clutter, I found it much easier to use than the previous Samsung S95F.

Perhaps more importantly, the S95H is a top performer when it comes to picture quality and settings. I could adjust the contrast and brightness to perfectly light famously dim shows like Game of Thrones. As an OLED, the blacks look richer and darker, more so than most RGB models. The AI optimization picture settings here are actually useful—during soccer matches, the TV adjust to make the pitch look even greener and minimizes background crowd noise, for example.

It's a bit pricey, but the overall brightness, contrast, color quality, and even built-in sound are all premium-grade.

The company famous for streaming sticks released its first OLED TV this year, and it follows the brand's formula of low-cost simplicity. Roku has, up until this point, stuck with LED TV models with average performance. Wonder of wonders, the Pro Series is not bad at all, making even dark scenes in movies like Solo: A Star Wars Story look vibrant and colorful. Outside of picture quality, Roku makes things as easy as possible, with features like Smart Picture Max, which automatically tweaks picture settings for you, a simple TV operating system (Roku OS, of course), and an uncluttered remote.

I will say, the brightness and contrast are good for this price, but nowhere near the cinema-quality color of something like the premium Samsung S95H. I think it's a great option for anyone on a budget or for people who only watch TV occasionally.

The Samsung The Frame Pro (2026) is my TV of the year, but the Amazon Ember Artline is also a capable, significantly cheaper, art TV. Just don't expert as premium of an image in movies and TV shows.

Art televisions use a matte finish on the screen to help make paintings look more realistic and textured. The Ember Artline achieves this look, and even includes frame bezel that snap into place around the screen (these are sold separately on Samsung's Frame TVs). I loved looking at painting on this TV, including some animated ones Amazon offers in the catalog. Using the TV is simple, and the improved Alexa+ voice assistant is useful for changing the volume (hands free) or finding obscure sci-fi films.

Image quality isn't the big selling point of this TV: the art, aesthetic, and low price are. Gamers will find the 60 Hz refresh rate lacking, especially for twitchy action titles. Contrast and brightness are okay, but not nearly as impressive as something like the Samsung The Frame Pro. But keep in mind: this TV is far, far cheaper than premium options.

While the LG Micro RGB Evo is endlessly tweakable and outperformed every other RGB model I tested for picture quality, the Sony BRAVIA 9 II RGB TV still takes the cake when it comes to gaming. That’s especially true if you own a Sony PlayStation 5, since the TV will automatically adjust the picture quality and latency to match the game console. I tested it mostly using a high-end PC, and at a 120 Hz refresh rate, latency felt non-existent to me.

I also found this TV to be a capable alternative to a premium OLED. Red, green, and blue colors are almost infinitely adjustable. During a scene in Toy Story 5 by a tree in a field, the sun creates splashes of color that look incredibly lush and vivid. Watching Game of Thrones, I found I could enable a special black level setting to make night battles look more realistic.

The Bravia 9 II uses Google TV OS and Google Gemini voice assistant, which both run simply, smoothly, and with no weird hiccups. While the LG Micro RGB Evo is a better performer for color and contrast, the BRAVIA 9 II’s gaming features, fast performance, high-end speakers, and deep blacks are exceptional.

Hisense UR9 RGB Mini-LED: My top pick for a midrange RGB, the Hisense UR9 has rich colors thanks to RGB tech shining red, green, and blue pixels. Some scenes, including ones in the movie The Last Duel, looked extra crisp and colorful. But it's not quite as excellent as my top picks.

LG B6 OLED: The LG B6 is a great budget-friendly OLED TV that performed very similarly to the Roku Pro Series OLED. Either one of them would serve you well, but we gave the nod to the Roku TV for it's lower price, simpler remote, and easy to use Roku operating system.

Samsung Micro RGB R95H: Samsung's Micro RGB display tech didn’t make the Samsung Micro RGB R95H stand out from the competition as much as I'd hoped. In fact, the LG Micro RGB Evo responded much better to picture quality adjustments, and while shows and movies looked colorful and clear, they weren't quite as jaw-dropping as similarly priced RGB and OLED competitors.

Sony Bravia 7 II: The Sony Bravia 7 II is unfortunately outclassed by the other midrange RGB TV on this list: the Hisense UR9. It is more expensive, it's harder to set up, and the picture quality doesn't quite match that of the Hisense TV.

Sony Bravia 8 II: Former WIRED reviewer Ryan Waniata tested this stunning high-end OLED, and praised it's top-notch image quality and processing. That said, the Samsung S95H is newer, about the same price, and has a more striking, glare-free image than the Sony Bravia 8 II.

TCL Nxtvision Series Art: This budget art TV simply cannot compete with similarly low-priced art TVs like the Amazon Ember Artline TV and Hisense Class S7 CanvasTV. Both offer better picture quality and a better general user experience. You can read my full review here.

TCL RM9L RGB Mini-LED: The TCL RM9L RGB TV is huge and hugely expensive. The $6,000 85-inch is the smallest and cheapest model you can get, and it is generally outclassed by the LG Micro RGB Evo.

The WIRED reviews team is busy testing the ever-popular midrange LG C6 and premium LG G6. Given past performances from LG C and G-series TVs, we expect them to be strong contenders for top accolades in this guide.

#375. A24 is having a great year at the box office. That could give HBO Max a streaming edge

Independent movie studio A24 has had a banner year at the box office, and HBO Max is set up to benefit from its success.

A24 is behind some of this year's buzziest films, including horror hit "Backrooms," dark comedy "The Drama" starring Zendaya and Robert Pattinson, and the Elizabeth Holmes documentary "You Can See Everything," co-directed by Nathan Fielder.

The studio has generated more than $526 million at the domestic box office this year as of Nov. 15, according to data from Rentrak. That's already roughly $290 million, or more than 50%, above its haul for all of 2025.

"They have an identity all their own, and just the mere mention of A24, the recognition that a movie is from A24, gives it instant credibility and provides a must-see factor, no matter what the subject matter," Paul Dergarabedian, head of marketplace trends at Rentrak, told CNBC.

Skydance co-CEO and Chairman David Ellison cited movie releases from A24 as part of the company's "unmatched portfolio" during its most recent earnings call.

A24 films released this year broke records at the box office, with "Backrooms" becoming the studio's biggest domestic opening to date and "You Can See Everything" notching the biggest documentary opening since "Fahrenheit 9/11" in 2004.

That success has already begun to translate to HBO Max's platform.

When "Backrooms" began streaming on HBO Max, it was the most streamed title on the platform for two weeks, according to Nielsen data. The film was also the fourth overall most streamed title the week it premiered, racking up 226 million minutes of viewing time.

After more than a year of competing bids and regulatory hurdles, Skydance now oversees two of the world's largest streaming platforms: HBO Max and Paramount+.

The company plans to eventually merge the streaming services into a single platform. It will take the first step in that effort by offering a value bundle in early 2027.

The combination of the platforms "will drive stronger engagement and higher lifetime value," co-CEO Ynon Kreiz said on the company's earnings call earlier this month.

Paramount Skydance's direct-to-consumer segment, which includes Paramount+ and its free, ad-supported channel, Pluto TV, generated more than $2 billion in revenue during the third quarter, representing more than 35% of total revenue for the period. That segment revenue marked an 11% year-over-year increase, with revenue from Paramount+ up 21%.

The earnings do not reflect the Warner Bros. Discovery acquisition, since that deal closed after the close of the quarter.

Revenue growth in streaming will be important as it faces the daunting task of managing nearly $80 billion of debt.

The company has said it expects to realize $6 billion in cost savings over the next three years and has put a particular focus on consolidating its operations and streamlining its marketing spend.

#374. The best free Black Friday deals: How to get Kindle+, Audible, Apple Music, bonus gift cards, and more for $0

Black Friday sales are live, and while everyone loves a good discount, nothing beats an unexpected freebie — especially when you're buying gifts for other people.

What's better than free money? Personally, I can't think of anything. Right now, anyone who buys select $100 Best Buy gift cards will earn a free $15 Best Buy voucher they can put toward a future purchase there. Choose from Regal, ChatGPT, Google Play, or Apple gift cards.

Heads up: As part of the Apple Store's Black Friday Event, you'll soon be able to score a free gift card worth up to $300 there when you buy select Apple devices. The offer goes live on Friday, Nov. 27 and runs through Nov. 30.

The Home Depot's BOGO Black Friday tool deal was a hit with Mashable readers last holiday season, so I'm pleased to report that it's back again. Just add certain on-sale cordless tools and kits to your cart to earn another free cordless tool worth up to $249. You can take your pick from impact drivers, saws, hammer drills, sanders, and more from popular brands like DeWalt, Makita, Milwaukee, Ridgid, and Ryobi.

Most of the best Black Friday deals are available online, so retailers have to pull out the stops to get people into their stores. And Lowe's is going hard with its free Black Friday Bucket giveaway for the second year in a row.

Here's how it works: The first 50 MyLowe’s Rewards members in line at every store will receive a bucket containing at least 10 free products and offers. Four of those 50 buckets will include a red, green, gold, or silver ticket that earns their possessor a grand prize: either a free $2,000 major appliance, an EGO outdoor power tool, a Craftsman tools package, or a Blackstone grilling package. If you can't show up right away, fret not: The next 100 people in line will get a miniature bucket containing $5 in MyLowe’s Money and other rewards.

The festivities kick off at 6 a.m. local time at more than 1,700 Lowe's stores. If you're not a MyLowe's Rewards member yet, you can sign up for free.

Bass Pro Shops and Cabela’s — The first 250 customers (ages 16 and older) at every store will receive a free mystery gift card worth $10 to $500, which will be valid from Dec. 6 to 24.

JCPenney — Select stores are giving away four prizes throughout the day, including a miniature Harry Potter snow globe, a Ninja air fryer, diamond earrings, and a Samsonite suitcase.

Michaels — Every store is giving away 500 "Countdown to Craftsmas" advent calendars. One calendar in every store contains a $100 gift card, and one recipient will win a $10,000 grand prize.

Sephora at Kohl's — The first 200 customers at select stores will receive a free Kohl’s Cash voucher worth $5 to $100 to spend on beauty purchases that day.

Target — The first 100 customers at every store will receive a free Target gift card worth $25, $50, or $100. One person per store will get a $1,000 gift card.

Paying for a membership just to shop a sale feels a little counterproductive. Luckily, eligible customers can try Amazon Prime free for 30 days. Starting your trial now gives you time to shop early deals and still have it for Black Friday and Cyber Monday. After the trial, Prime costs $14.99 per month or $139 per year, depending on your selected plan.

Prime comes with more than free shipping, though that’s probably the perk you’ll use most while shopping for gifts. You also get Prime Video, Amazon Music’s ad-free listening options, access to a selection of books through Prime Reading, and member-exclusive deals. The newest addition is $0 delivery fees on eligible Uber Eats restaurant orders of $25 or more placed through Amazon — a useful extra for the nights you’d rather order dinner than make it.

Books are one of those things I don’t particularly enjoy putting a spending limit on. A subscription at least gives you a way to read more without paying for every title separately. Kindle+, formerly Kindle Unlimited, offers a 30-day free trial with access to a catalog of ebooks, audiobooks, magazines, and comics. It automatically renews at $11.99 per month unless you cancel.

You might also see an offer for two months for $0.99 total. That’s not free, but it’s worth comparing with the trial before you choose. The best tech deal this week The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile

The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile

And despite the name, you don’t need an iPhone to use it — Apple Music also works on Android and Windows.

Spotify Premium Individual — One month free for people who haven’t tried Premium before, then $12.99 per month. Includes ad-free music and offline downloads.

Deezer Family — One month free, then $19.99 per month. Cancel anytime.

Not all reading has to involve sitting down with a book. Audible’s 30-day free trial lets new customers choose one audiobook from its collection, including bestsellers and new releases, and listen to an included catalog of podcasts. After the trial, it automatically renews at $8.99 per month unless you cancel.

There’s also a separate promotion for three months at $0.99 per month, plus a $20 Audible bonus. I wouldn’t call that free, but paying $2.97 for three months might make more sense than taking one free month and then paying the regular rate.

Hoopla — Free through participating public libraries. Check whether your library offers access before signing up; this is library borrowing, not a subscription trial that turns into a monthly bill.

Kobo Plus Listen — 14 days free, then $7.99 per month. The Read & Listen plan includes both ebooks and audiobooks for $9.99 per month after the trial. You can use the Kobo Books app on your phone or tablet, so there’s no need to buy an e-reader.

Everand — 30 days free, with plans starting at $11.99 per month afterward. The trial includes one premium-title unlock, plus unlimited access to a separate catalog of more than 20,000 audiobooks, ebooks, and podcasts.

All You Can Books — 30 days free, then $24.99 per month. The service advertises unlimited downloads from its catalog of audiobooks, ebooks, language courses, and other content, and says downloaded files remain yours even after cancellation.

I’d use the free month to check whether the publications you actually want to read are included. A long list of magazines sounds nice, but it doesn’t mean much if you’re only opening one of them.

After the trial, the subscription costs $14.99 per month, so it's worth setting a reminder to cancel if you don't plan on keeping it.

If you've been thinking about switching phone providers, Verizon is also offering a 30-day free trial, giving you a chance to test its network without switching providers. You can keep your existing phone number and continue using your current network while trying Verizon through an eSIM. There's no credit card required, no contract, and no need to remember to cancel, either. The trial automatically expires after 30 days, so you won't be charged if you decide not to switch.

T-Mobile — 30 days free for eligible non-T-Mobile customers with a compatible, unlocked device. Includes access to T-Mobile's network, satellite coverage, and member benefits, with no credit card, credit check, or commitment required.

Visible — 15 days free with unlimited data, talk, text, and hotspot access on Verizon's network. No credit card, contract, or automatic renewal required.

AT&T Wireless — 30 days free with unlimited talk and text, plus 100GB of data. Keep your current phone, number, and service while testing the network. Compatible iPhone or Android required.

And if you're planning to pick up a new Apple device during the Black Friday sales, you could get an even better deal, with three months free when you purchase an eligible device.

Glo — 7 days free, with access to more than 12,000 on-demand yoga, Pilates, meditation, and strength classes led by over 60 instructors.

Peloton App — Free trial for new members, with access to thousands of workout classes across more than 15 exercise types, including options that don't require equipment. Cancel anytime.

Ladder — 7 days free, with access to all training plans, personalized workout recommendations, introductory classes, and fitness communities. No payment information required to start the trial.

Nike Training Club — Completely free, with access to guided workouts, multi-week training programs, and fitness advice. No subscription or trial period required.

If you're looking for a way to unwind after a busy day, Calm is offering a seven-day free trial of its Premium membership. You'll get access to more than 50,000 minutes of content, including guided meditations, Sleep Stories, relaxing music, and nature sounds. After the trial, the subscription automatically renews at $79.99 per year, plus applicable taxes, so make sure you cancel before the seven days are up if you don't want to continue.

Black Friday sales are live, and while everyone loves a good discount, nothing beats an unexpected freebie — especially when you're buying gifts for other people.

What's better than free money? Personally, I can't think of anything. Right now, anyone who buys select $100 Best Buy gift cards will earn a free $15 Best Buy voucher they can put toward a future purchase there. Choose from Regal, ChatGPT, Google Play, or Apple gift cards.

Heads up: As part of the Apple Store's Black Friday Event, you'll soon be able to score a free gift card worth up to $300 there when you buy select Apple devices. The offer goes live on Friday, Nov. 27 and runs through Nov. 30.

The Home Depot's BOGO Black Friday tool deal was a hit with Mashable readers last holiday season, so I'm pleased to report that it's back again. Just add certain on-sale cordless tools and kits to your cart to earn another free cordless tool worth up to $249. You can take your pick from impact drivers, saws, hammer drills, sanders, and more from popular brands like DeWalt, Makita, Milwaukee, Ridgid, and Ryobi.

Most of the best Black Friday deals are available online, so retailers have to pull out the stops to get people into their stores. And Lowe's is going hard with its free Black Friday Bucket giveaway for the second year in a row.

Here's how it works: The first 50 MyLowe’s Rewards members in line at every store will receive a bucket containing at least 10 free products and offers. Four of those 50 buckets will include a red, green, gold, or silver ticket that earns their possessor a grand prize: either a free $2,000 major appliance, an EGO outdoor power tool, a Craftsman tools package, or a Blackstone grilling package. If you can't show up right away, fret not: The next 100 people in line will get a miniature bucket containing $5 in MyLowe’s Money and other rewards.

The festivities kick off at 6 a.m. local time at more than 1,700 Lowe's stores. If you're not a MyLowe's Rewards member yet, you can sign up for free.

Target — The first 100 customers at every store will receive a free Target gift card worth $25, $50, or $100. One person per store will get a $1,000 gift card.
