#241. Half of NASA's aging Mars fleet knocked offline by technical issues

Perseverance is having trouble transmitting to Earth. Odyssey is rapidly burning through its waning fuel supply.

Two of NASA’s four missions operating at Mars have suspended science operations after encountering separate technical issues in recent weeks.

The missions affected by the outages—hopefully temporary—are NASA’s Perseverance rover and Odyssey orbiter. Both are operating beyond their original design lifetimes. Perseverance is in its sixth year exploring the surface of Mars, having collected rock and soil samples for eventual return to Earth. The rover is now studying the rim of a crater that once contained an ancient lake of liquid water. Odyssey arrived in orbit around Mars in 2001 and is the longest-lived Mars mission in history.

The problem on Perseverance stems from the rover’s communications system. The rover has two redundant UHF radios for high-rate communications with a fleet of orbiters that relay data to Earth. A separate X-band system is available for direct-to-Earth communications at a lower data rate.

One of the rover’s two UHF radios was unresponsive when it powered up on October 30, triggering an automatic switch to the backup radio and placing the rover in safe mode. Ground teams at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in California later discovered the backup UHF radio was transmitting at about half of its expected power output, NASA said in a statement last week.

“The team has stopped using both radios until they can evaluate potential causes of the issues and one or both are deemed safe to resume operating,” NASA said.

Perseverance is now transmitting signals directly to Earth in X-band, but the connection provides a “significantly lower data rate” than relaying signals through orbiters using the UHF radios. Mission managers paused the rover’s science operations “out of an abundance of caution” as they investigate the radio problem. Their initial focus is on getting the backup UHF radio running before turning their attention to recovering the primary radio, NASA said.

“The team is hopeful the rover could return to science by the end of November.”

The six-wheeled robot broke a record last month for the farthest any vehicle has driven on another planet. The Perseverance rover surpassed the 28.06-mile (45.16-kilometer) mark set by NASA’s Opportunity rover, which stopped working in 2018. Perseverance’s odometer now sits at twice the rover’s original goal for distance traveled.

The situation with the Odyssey orbiter seems more dire. One of the four reaction wheels used for pointing the spacecraft stopped spinning in early November, leaving Odyssey with two good wheels after the first one failed in 2013. The orbiter needs at least three wheels to keep it oriented correctly.

“Without the three reaction wheels, the spacecraft must rely solely on its hydrazine thrusters to remain oriented,” NASA said. The orbiter requires stable pointing to turn its solar arrays toward the Sun and its science instruments toward Mars.

Odyssey was running low on propellant before the reaction wheel malfunction, but managers were optimistic that with “extremely low” fuel usage, the orbiter would have enough to continue operating through at least the end of 2028, said Jeffrey Plaut, Odyssey’s project scientist at JPL, in a presentation earlier this year.

That assumed no failures in Odyssey’s three remaining reaction wheels. Without three healthy wheels, engineers estimate the spacecraft has enough hydrazine fuel to last one to two months, NASA said. The good news is that ground teams had some initial success troubleshooting the balky reaction wheel. Further testing is necessary to determine whether the wheel is recoverable.

Odyssey is one of four orbiters NASA uses to relay data between Earth and the Perseverance and Curiosity rovers on the Martian surface. Curiosity is still driving and collecting data after 14 years on Mars. The other three relay craft are NASA’s Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter, which reached the red planet in 2006, the European Space Agency’s 10-year-old ExoMars Trace Gas Orbiter, and ESA’s 23-year-old Mars Express spacecraft.

NASA lost contact with its MAVEN orbiter last December after 11 years of operations at Mars when the spacecraft suddenly spun out of control. An investigation could not identify a specific root cause, but engineers concluded that a radiation-induced single event upset or a software issue caused MAVEN’s flight computer to reboot, according to Tiffany Morgan, director of NASA’s robotic Mars Exploration Program.

MAVEN’s inertial measurement unit failed to provide the computer with correct information on the spacecraft’s orientation, causing it to spin in response to the faulty data, Morgan said in a November 9 presentation to the Mars Exploration Program Analysis Group.

NASA is preparing to send reinforcements to renew the agency’s presence at Mars. In September, NASA awarded Blue Origin a $700 million contract for the Mars Telecommunications Network (MTN), an orbiter dedicated to providing high-bandwidth connectivity between Earth and other missions operating on and around the red planet.

NASA wanted Blue Origin to complete the telecom orbiter by the end of 2028 and have it operational at Mars in 2030. But the Mars Telecommunications Network is on hold after Rocket Lab, which lost its bid to win the MTN contract, filed a protest with the Government Accountability Office. The GAO is expected to rule on the protest next month, at which time Blue Origin could start work on the NASA contract if the government rejects Rocket Lab’s petition.

Another Mars mission, SkyFall, could also launch in 2028. NASA aims to send three helicopter drones to Mars to explore the planet’s geology and weather from the air.

A perennial priority for Mars scientists is replacing the unique high-resolution mapping camera on the aging Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter. Such a capability will help identify landing sites for future robotic and human missions, including a potential mission to return Perseverance’s rock specimens to Earth.

NASA is in the very early stages of developing a mission concept that could take over MRO’s imaging capability, but there’s no firm schedule or budget for such an undertaking. NASA will likely rely on MRO for landing-site reconnaissance well into the 2030s.

Ars Technica has been separating the signal from the noise for over 25 years. With our unique combination of technical savvy and wide-ranging interest in the technological arts and sciences, Ars is the trusted source in a sea of information. After all, you don’t need to know everything, only what’s important.

#240. Black Friday streaming deals 2026: The best deals live now and what to expect

As in other markets, 2026 was a year of price hikes in the streaming world. The majority of our favorite streamers bumped up the costs of subscriptions this year, including Peacock, Apple TV, Disney+, Hulu, Netflix, ESPN, and Paramount+. Viewers everywhere are looking for the chance to save some money, so the slate of Black Friday streaming deals has arrived in the nick of time.

As Mashable's resident streaming expert, I've been tracking streaming prices for years now. There's absolutely no doubt that Black Friday is the best time of year to sign up and save on that wallet strain. I'm pumped that despite all of the price hikes in 2026, it's proving to be another banger year for streaming deals. I highly recommend taking advantage of these prices while they're available, particularly if you're looking to diversify your viewing and try out a new platform. The truth is that we're unlikely to see discounts this steep for a while.

Most streaming deals for major streaming services went live early during Black Friday week, but I'll certainly be keeping an eye out for any more that roll in. Most deals expire on Nov. 30, aka Cyber Monday, unless otherwise noted. So don't hesitate to secure the offer ASAP.

Below, find my top picks for the best Black Friday streaming deals of 2026.

Black Friday 2026 live blog: Top deals, store hours, and real-time updates

The HBO Max Black Friday deal is top dog once again in the streaming world. This year, you can secure an entire year of streaming for half the usual cost. That drops it to just $5.49 per month, or $65.88 total for the year. Better yet, the offer is available as a standalone deal, a Prime Video add-on, or a Roku subscription.

Yes, you'll have to watch with ads, but for the price, it's easy to look past that. With a Basic subscription, you also won't get access to live sports. I'm going to be completely upfront about this: most streaming deals aren't going to change your finances in any significant way. The truth is that Black Friday streaming deals have gotten steadily less impressive over the past few years. It's also worth noting that most deals apply only to the ad-supported tiers (with a few exceptions). Still, any and every discount is welcome in a time when prices keep rising. Every cent counts, and it's easy to lose track of just how much you spend across various streaming services.

Most streamers have announced their Black Friday deals at this point, but you may be wondering if there's more to come. Aside from some stragglers later this week, I would say the best streaming deals have already arrived.

I'm shocked that Peacock's Black Friday deal is as good as it is for 2026. Last year, the streamer didn't offer a deal at all, so this is light-years better than I was expecting. If you've been holding off on subscribing, now is likely the only time you'll get a decent discount. The Paramount+, HBO Max, and Disney+/Hulu Black Friday offers are pretty much on par with their deals of years past. I would lock in HBO Max and the Disney+/Hulu bundle for a full year, as more price increases could pop up in 2027. Paramount+ tends to offer discounts throughout the year more than any other streamer, so if you miss out on this one, it's no biggie.

It's not worth holding on for a Netflix Black Friday deal, unfortunately. Netflix has never offered a Black Friday discount, or any kind of discount for that matter. #237. Domestic violence soars to record high in Germany

Every three days in Germany, a man kills his wife or ex-partner. Every 10 minutes, the police record a sexual offense against a woman. "A shocking finding," according to Justice Minister Stefanie Hubig.

The German government has presented some grim statistics with regard to misogyny, rape, violence and murder, with reported cases of domestic violence at an all-time high.

At a press conference in Berlin on Tuesday, Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt, Family Affairs Minister Karin Prien and Justice Minister Stefanie Hubig released the latest figures on crimes that specifically target women: whether within families and intimate relationships, in public or online.

In contrast to the statistics pertaining to crime overall, which have remained the same or increased only slightly, reports of crimes against women have increased.

"Behind all these terrible numbers lie individual stories, people and particularly women and girls, whose lives are severely affected by these acts of violence," said Dobrindt.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

In 2025, some 280,000 people were victims of physical abuse in their own homes, a 2.8% increase compared to the previous year. Over 70% of the victims were female. Each hour, 16 women are subjected to physical abuse behind closed doors.

The male victims included boys who had been assaulted by their fathers.

The number of misogynistic hate crimes has also risen dramatically, by almost 50%, to 819 cases.

"The figures show us what it can mean to be a woman in Germany," said Hubig. "It can mean being killed by one's partner or ex-partner. Being a woman can also mean being physically abused by one's partner or ex-partner in one's own home. Being a woman can mean that one's sexual autonomy is brutally disregarded."

According to the latest findings, both perpetrators and victims are getting younger. In 2025, nearly half of all female victims of sexual offenses were under the age of 18. And the number of incidents of online violence against women and girls rose by 15.7%. This includes the unauthorized sharing of videos and photos, verbal abuse, manipulation of images, threats and online blackmail, as well as cyberstalking.

Because many perpetrators and victims are still in their teens, Prien, who is also minister for education, said the government wanted to focus primarily on schools, which she explained should become places of prevention.

"Ultimately, we need to bring about a change in people's mindsets, especially those of men. That will be the deciding factor in the end," she said.

Over the weekend, Justice Minister Hubig had already announced that in future all femicides, the intentional killing of girls and women because of their gender, would be classified as murders. Currently, such crimes are often classified as manslaughter, for which the penalty is less severe than for murder.

Hubig told German broadcaster ZDF that it was increasingly common that femicides be described as family tragedies or as domestic dramas revolving around jealousy and then classified as manslaughter.

Martina Link, the vice president of the Federal Criminal Police Office, was also at the press conference in Berlin. She called for everybody to pay closer attention to the issue, within their own families, neighborhoods or at work.

"Violence against women is not a private matter," she said. "Not in our immediate surroundings nor in the digital world."

She also pointed out that when it came to sexual offenses and domestic violence, only about 5-10% of cases were reported.

This article was originally written in German.
